subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT FUNDING FOR TRAINING FACILITIES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. To meet the shortage of skilled workers in Canada, and in view of the fact that at present most training costs for an apprentice fall on the training company and many firms do not have apprenticeship or on-the-job training programs because they are too costly, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers):
That the federal government institute a fairer plan for paying for facilities, instructors and equipment, and since the early stage of apprenticeship is a kind of post-secondary education and is vital to the economy, that the federal government pay a greater share of this training.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF HERD MAINTENANCE PROGRAM-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the criteria set out to determine eligibility for the herd maintenance assistance program were unfair, inconsistent and discriminatory toward northeastern Alberta producers. Recommendations concerning this injustice from the Herd Maintenance Review Board fell on deaf ministerial ears. In addition to being denied herd assistance, farmers in northeastern Alberta suffered a disastrous 1980-81 winter followed by an unusually dry summer. In view of these facts, and given that the 1981 Liberal budget offers virtually no assistance to Canadian farmers struggling to survive against high interest rates and poor returns, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga):
That this House direct the Ministers of Finance, Agriculture and Regional Economic Expansion to extend the herd maintenance assistance program or to create a new, meaningful and fair program which will allow producers in this country to maintain their herds.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In contrast to other workers like plumbers and carpenters, Section 16 of the Unemployment Insurance Act denies farm workers all unemployment insurance credit for the days worked unless they work 25 days for the same employer. Thus, over 100,000 farm workers among Canada's poorest paid workers who are not normally covered by minimum wage legislation, health and safety protection, or workers' compensation benefits, are vie-

That Section 16 of the Unemployment Insurance Act be abolished since it discriminates against a racial minority who do at least half the farm work in the Fraser Valley and because it has been described as a "Magna Carta for unscrupulous labour practices".

subsubtopic: CALL FOR REDUCTION IN BANK RATE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker,
I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The Liberal government has repeatedly told Canadians that its high interest rate policy can be attributed to United States interest rates. Last Thursday the Bank of Canada dropped its rate only 1/100th of a percentage point, to 15.31 per cent, while in the U.S. the Federal Reserve Bank reduced its discount rate a full percentage point, from 13 per cent to 12 per cent. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby):
That this government be consistent in its interest rate policy and direct the Bank of Canada to drop its bank rate at least two percentage points to reduce the spread between Canadian and the United States interest rates.

subsubtopic: INTEREST CHARGEABLE ON NATIONAL DEBT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise in my place to ask a question of the Minister of Finance. The minister will know that on page 12 of the Auditor General's report, in talking about the interest on the national debt, he says that paying that interest "accounts for more than one fifth of every tax dollar, and its load burdens all the people of Canada like a huge, high-interest mortgage." Some 20 cents out of every dollar, Madam Speaker, go to the bankers in Geneva, New York, and throughout Canada, so that bankers through investments receive more money than we spend on pensions, health care or post-secondary education. The solution is an issue of "political will", according to the Auditor General.
Can the finance minister give us an indication that he and his party are going to demonstrate the political will necessary to reduce the national debt and provide this country with more money for pensions, health care, and things of that kind?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INTEREST CHARGEABLE ON NATIONAL DEBT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, like the Auditor General I am concerned at the size of the national debt, and particularly the proportion of annual outlays that have to be spent to service the debt in the form of interest payments.
I disagree with the hon. member when he says that all these payments flow outside the country. I believe that is what I heard him say. There are many Canadians who hold Canada Savings Bonds and other debt instruments. A good deal of the debt is within the country-I would say almost all of it.
The hon. member is asking for an expression of political will. I believe I have demonstrated that political will in the budget when I indicated that next year my financial requirements will be reduced to $6.6 billion. If the hon. member will recall, earlier in the session, for the current year I introduced a bill asking for borrowing authority in the net amount of about $11 billion. The next bill will ask for $6.6 billion. I believe that is a rather substantial demonstration of my determination to reduce that proportion of total outlays assigned to the national debt.

subsubtopic: INTEREST CHARGEABLE ON NATIONAL DEBT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

My supplementary question is for the President of the Treasury Board. The Auditor General on that same page indicates that one of the ways to reduce the deficit and reduce those interest payments is to reduce waste in government spending, and he says the key to that is "dedicated support of their ministers", that is, dedicated support to the civil servants on the issue of cutting wasteful spending. Can the President of the Treasury Board indicate to and promise this House that in a discussion with the Prime Minister of Canada prior to the shuffling of his cabinet, he will advise the Prime Minister to fire those ministers who are not concerned about economy and cutting down waste, and promote some backbenchers who perhaps are a little bit more concerned about cutting waste?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the adjournment debate started last night, I informed the House of a proposal according to which an economic summit should be organized as soon as possible in Sherbrooke. I said that it would give us a chance to determine the condition of the various economic sectors in Sherbrooke and decide how we want our region to develop.
We cannot let decisions affecting our economy be made without having a say in their implementation. My suggestion for an economic summit means that someone will have to be in charge of organizing the summit. Without wishing to give anyone in particular a mandate or a set of tasks, or responsibilities, it seems to me that the industrial commissariat, in view of its fundamental role in Sherbrooke's economic development, would be able to organize a summit with the help of all economic partners in Sherbrooke. Personally, I am prepared to co-operate fully with the organizers of such a meeting.
Mr. Speaker, on a different matter, I would like to say something about the VIA Rail cutbacks announced in the last week of July by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). As soon as the government announced its intentions, I sent a telegram to the minister in which I expressed my apprehension as follows;
I read in the newspapers that in the near future, your department intends to terminate VIA Rail services between Sherbrooke and Montreal. I cannot support such a proposal. I should appreciate it if public hearings were held on this matter and the government's decision postponed until the local residents have aired their views on the present rail services provided for Sherbrooke and the general area.
Many organizations in the area and a number of private citizens informed me that they were opposed to the decision, and one of the agencies that has been most active in this respect, the Eastern Townships Regional Development Council, informed the minister in a brief and in press releases of that agency's position which reflects the region's concerns.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, and the minister has said as much many times in the House, that some passenger lines in Canada are not profitable. In a letter I received not long ago from VIA Rail, in reply to questions I asked the Director of Government Relations, Mr. Branchaud, I was informed that for the line Sherbrooke-Montreal-Sherbfooke, the user^rate averaged 30 per cent, but also that for Otterburn Park, Beloeil and Saint-Hyacinthe, the occupancy rate was 100 per cent, dropping after Saint-Hyacinthe to less than 25 per cent, that operating costs were $1.5 million and revenue only ^mounted to $140,-

December 8, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Pelletier
000, which means that on the VIA Rail route between Sherbrooke and Montreal, the railway company is losing more than $1.3 million per year. I also asked VIA Rail authorities whether they could put an LRC on the line between Sherbrooke and Montreal, and they answered that there were only eighty-eight cars of that type in Canada, that they were in high demand elsewhere in Canada, on relatively short routes, and that they could hardly justify putting another unit train on this route because of the low user rate.
I also asked whether it would be possible to establish a quicker route between Sherbrooke and Montreal and I was told that this was impossible as there is no continuous rail on a direct route, but that a project for a bus service between Sherbrooke and Drummondville, from where passengers could then go on to Montreal and Quebec, was being considered. Mr. Speaker, outside Montreal and Quebec city, Sherbrooke has been one of the busiest stops of the passenger service for over a century. I recognize that the figures provided to us for the last two decades show a substantial drop in the user rate between Sherbrooke and Montreal, but since our region is already manufacturing passenger cars for other countries and for VIA Rail, we believe in the Eastern Townships that an alternative must be found if it is not possible to maintain the present service, which is scheduled for abandonment in September 1982. We have to look at other solutions, and in my humble opinion, RDC passenger cars would be perfectly appropriate to the needs of our region. We shall continue to make representations to VIA Rail and the Department of Transport asking that an adequate solution be found to this problem before September, 1982, when the service between Sherbrooke and Montreal is scheduled to be abandoned.
Mr. Speaker, the problem of the footwear industry is reaching tragic proportions in many cities and villages throughout Canada. Nearly 4,000 workers have been laid off since the beginning of 1981. Reports published in 1977 and 1981 following the comprehensive and detailed studies made by the Antidumping Tribunal recognized that the Canadian footwear manufacturers had been seriously disadvantaged by the loopholes contained in the legislation. Both reports of the Antidumping Tribunal suggested that the government take effective action to protect the footwear industry as a whole. Mr. Speaker, imports now account for over 61 per cent of the Canadian market, and I find this completely unacceptable. In my humble opinion, it is essential that the government seriously consider comprehensive quotas, which are much more effective, and I believe that if the system is not weakened by administrative procedures as it has been in the past, the effectiveness and competitive ability of this industry will be greatly increased. I share the opinion expressed recently by Mr. Maheux in a letter to us in which he said:
We believe, and many experts agree, that the footwear manufacturing industry in Canada can be extremely vigorous, effective and better off competitively through an increased use of computers, and that it can become a positive
element in the Canadian economy during the eighties if the federal government decides to extend comprehensive quotas for a period of five to ten years.
Mr. Speaker, in that industry just as in the textile industry a larger share of the Canadian market must be opened to Canadian manufacturers. And above all, let no one argue that we are not giving enough chances to the poor countries which are anxious to compete on the Canadian market. In the majority of cases the developed countries are those which are now causing the most damage to the Canadian market. Mr. Speaker, I must say that today the minister is meeting with a good number of shoe manufacturers and that he answered a question I put to him in the House last week by saying that he was prepared to listen to representations from the industry and, if possible, to bring in amendments to the policy on footwear.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that it is imperative that the minister seriously consider some of the amendments advocated at this time by Canadian manufacturers and, since he is meeting with them today, I hope he will understand the plight of thousands of Quebecers and Canadians who work in that industry and who need to be reassured that the Canadian government will not now let that industry down by implementing the policy which has already been announced because, in my humble opinion, it will be quite vulnerable. Mr. Speaker, I see that my time has run out.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this budget has been called an economic disaster and a blunder of the first magnitude. Even the Liberal members recognize that now. I will refer to the hon. member for York-East (Mr. Collenette) in a moment or two if he will just be patient, because I designed part of my speech to accommodate him. I said it was a blunder. It is a blunder of the first magnitude. Of that there can be no doubt. It warrants the appellation a "blunder budget". When the minister came into the House the other night, with great fanfare, great cheers-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And a new pair of shoes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -and a new pair of shoes, and unveiled his budget, he dropped a real clinker. It landed with a dull thud which is still being heard throughout the country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Never in living memory has a budget been received with such universal criticism and disdain and such downright rejection. Those in trouble over mortgage payments, nearly one million Canadians, those in trouble over high interest bank loans, those who have been laid off and the farmers, all scrutinized the minister's announcement in a vain search for some small recognition of their desperate plight. Oh, there were lots of words: words of hope, words of good cheer and words conveying the message that help was on the way. That is what the minister responsible for housing said.
December 8, 1981

When the nature of the help was revealed, what was it? It was verbal cosmetics; nothing more and nothing less. It was a pallid, lacklustre attempt to convey an assurance of concern.
There is no concern in this budget and no milk of human kindness. It is a company report, a document exhibiting no care by a government with a total lack of care. It reads as though it were put together in a vacuum, so totally divorced is it from the real concerns of Canadians. It is quite obvious that to the minister and the gang of seven who put together the economic development formula at Meach Lake, the hardships and fears of the one million laid off and the 40,000 worrying about suddenly escalating mortgage payments were deemed to be very trivial indeed.
I now refer to the hon. member for York East. The other day we listened to him. He is highly regarded in philosophical circles in the Liberal Party. He explained his party's thoughts concerning those who were in trouble because of high interest rates. As a model of heartlessness and disregard for the facts, his speech was in a class by itself. He was placing the onus on the purchasers, and I think I quote him accurately, to look at their own financial situation. That was his remedy. He asked rhetorically, "Is it the duty of the government to subsidize lifestyle? Certainly not", he said. However, I say to him that it is the duty of the government, in a well managed economy, to so order its affairs that citizens will be assured of a measure of economic stability when they undertake large obligations and that they will not have the rug pulled out from under them by the mismanagement and indifference of an uncaring government.
This morning, on "Canada AM", the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) and his colleague were asked a very blunt but highly intelligent question by Pamela Wallin. She asked, "Why are you voting for a budget that is so roundly condemned?" "Oh", said the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, "we are not voting for all of these 120-odd budget resolutions. They are all going to come before the House and we will be voting on them. What we are voting on tonight has nothing to do with what is coming in the next month or two. We are just voting on a policy."

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame, shame!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member is not so stupid that he does not know the falsity of that kind of stand. What he and his colleagues are voting on tonight are all of those resolutions which will be before us in the weeks and months to come which are being authorized by this very budget. I know he did not pull the wool over Pamela Wallin's eyes, although I am sure he would have dearly loved to do so.
However, let us not try to pull the wool over the eyes of thousands of listeners to that broadcast. With regard to mortgage renewals, will he say that the mortgage renewal policy is not part of this budget? Does he condone what is happening to the mortgagors in this country who have been kicked out in the streets, or is that not a part of this budget policy? Will he be voting against the taxation of insurance premiums, or is that just a part of a resolution which will come along somewhere
The Budget-Mr. Nielsen
down the line? What utter tripe! I heard that hon. member this morning on "Canada AM" and I could not believe my ears. That is perhaps why he was not invited back into the cabinet after being left out in the cold. He was ceremoniously booted out.
The government's servile and heartless policy of high interest rates at 18 per cent-and that is a high interest rate-has condemned thousands of innocent people to suffer, to lose their savings, and to accept a deterioration in living standards. That is what the hon. member would be voting against tonight, unless he is for it, in which case he and his colleague the hon. member for York East will stand up and be counted on the side of implementation of that kind of heartless, uncaring policy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame, shame!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is exactly what Canadians are complaining about, and that is exactly the message the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) heard the other night from over 30 members of the Liberal caucus with whom he met after coming back from traipsing around Scotland and playing footsies with haggis and golf balls. The minister talked about restraint and equity.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Footsies?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have nothing against haggis. I am sorry, I did not intend it as a racial slur at all, quite the contrary.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope not.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not like it, mind you, but I respect the taste of the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) for haggis, at any rate.
When the minister presented his budget, he talked about restraint and equity. The words fell strangely from his lips as he spoke of increasing government spending by 22 per cent, taking $1 billion out of the economy in oil and gas taxes, and increasing his tax levies by $1.4 billion. If that is restraint, heaven help us if he ever lets go! Heaven help us if he ever takes the lid off!
There is restraint for everyone but the government. That is the policy of the government. Government members fly in formation to Winnipeg in three separate JetStars to attend the same function, for the same purpose, but they talk of restraint. The government goes ahead with its grandiose schemes for harnessing the economy-and that is the phrase it uses-for taking over resources from the provinces, for muscling in on business and industry, because, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) says, "If the free market is not working very well, we will have to do something about it".
This government goes about its endless empire-building like a mole tunnelling in the earth, surfacing only when it needs more money to carry on borrowing further. Its requirements are endless. Close to $70 billion in the expenditure program in this budget have been allocated for purposes and objectives which remain in what I consider to be the realm of the
13840

December 8, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Nielsen
airy-fairy. It is the development formula produced by the Meach Lake bunch. What is that formula?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Airy-fairy!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is more and more expenditures for less and less results. The economy spins in an ever-narrowing circle. The bankruptcy parade goes on. The army of lay-offs and jobless grows, and the government gets fatter and fatter and does less and less. The government members are the lotus-eaters. The lotus-eaters grow fat, and ordinary Canadians, hassled by fear and uncertainty, do not know where to turn. That is the crime of this budget. It is a Shylock budget. It helps no one but the money lenders. The government preaches restraint, but then squeezes the economy like a sponge for its own debatable purposes and to indulge in its own ideological pretentions about managing the economy and manipulating the social structure. This budget virtually flattens the middle-class in this country. It lowers the living standards and expectations of millions of Canadians, wiping out savings accounts and their future hopes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do you believe that?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, indeed I believe that with all the fervour at my command, more than the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River believed himself when he appeared on "Canada AM" this morning. He said that when he was going to vote for this budget, he was not going to be voting for all of these miseries that will be brought down on the heads of so many millions of Canadians. Yes, I believe it, more than he can honestly say he believed what he said this morning.
Giving the government an additional $2 billion in energy tax and additional taxation to play with is like giving a drunk a credit card for the liquor store. Sometimes it makes me wonder whether or not members on the other side might have such credit cards and are using them regularly.
Meanwhile, at the consumer level where stimulus is required, the dead hand of the government has come down hard. The palsied hand of this government is digging deeper into the pockets of Canadians more than any other government has in our history in order to seize whatever disposable income is left to them through so-called loopholes. In this regard, the government's approach is very like that of the mafia. Whatever it does not pick up is now defined as a loophole. The government is actually and literally taxing the teeth in people's mouths.
Canadians, hit with a whole series of higher taxes-and I wonder if the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is going to vote for that-are also being forced, to pay an extra $1,500 annually to heat their homes and drive their cars so that this government can squeeze an additional $1 billion out of the economy. That is $1,500 for people in southern Canada, Mr. Speaker. It is far more than that in the north. Imagine how this budget hits the north. Can members imagine just how hard it hits those people living north of 60 where heating and
transport are not luxuries but necessities of life, indeed, matters of life and death in the more remote Arctic communities? This hidden tax will add $2,500 annually to the cost of living of the average northerner and a great deal more for those in the more remote northern areas. This serves as a further disincentive to living north of 60 and it shows this government's total disregard for the future of northern Canada.
And still, as ministers drive around in their limousines to their $2,000 lunches or fly their individual jets in formation to party seminars, we hear the refrain "Restraint, restraint, for the end of the world is at hand". Then a few days before the election, the Meach Lake boys, the gang of seven, spent $130,000 boasting about how the government had spent $30 billion in 18 months. That is restraint? It is not the economy that needs to be restrained, sir, it is this government.
Then we had the egregious blunder of taxing assembly costs on residential housing construction which threatened to freeze 20,000 housing starts across the country. The minister, and I see him in his seat now, backed off when that matter was brought to his attention by the leader of this party. It was the first he had heard of it, although he had heard about a good many other things in the budget that somehow got out of his hands.
This raises the question of how many other situations of economic disaster have remained outside the minister's knowledge. Perhaps he just is not informed, or perhaps he just does not grasp the impact of his tax measures until disaster strikes. He should be in a position about now to realize that the budget is shoving this country into a serious recession, and that as the United States starts out of recession in the spring, we will be plunging down the slope, urged on by this feckless, tired and tattered government.
The budget simply tightens the screws on Canadians all across this land. Never was so much verbosity expended to achieve so little. The government's vaunted economic strategy can be summed up as "Loser takes all". They are steering this country to disaster amid a stream of cliches.
The Prime Minister, while addressing the party faithful a few weeks ago in one of the interim periods when he was not battling with Mr. Levesque, said this:
Canadians must come to their senses.
Canadians have been waiting for this government to come to its senses for a long time.
In his budget speech the minister dipped deep into the cliche department when he said:
It is time to overcome our anxieties.
No doubt this was addressed to the thousands of people who have lost their jobs, the thousands who have lost their homes or the thousands who have seen their businesses go into bankruptcy. The chief anxiety suffered by most Canadians at this time is a government completely out of step with the rest of the country and with the needs of the country; a government marching to a different drum.
December 8, 1981

It would take a great many doses of MacEachen soothing syrup to calm the uneasiness that exists in the economy at the present time. At a time when hundreds of thousands of Canadians are feeling the pinch of economic hardship, this budget is a positive indecency. It constitutes a betrayal by the government of the assurances given in this House to home owners by the minister responsible for housing and others in the cabinet. "Wait for the budget" was the cry of the minister in charge of housing and the Minister of Finance. "Wait for the budget and all will be well'. Home owners waited and waited, but they waited in vain. There is nothing in this budget to assist one single home owner in weathering the storm of high interest rates, only cosmetic guarantees.
The minister has accomplished the nearly incredible feat of increasing inflation while slowing down the economy and producing rising unemployment. This makes him a destroyer of the dreams and hopes of thousands of Canadians, a destroyer without mercy, without concern, without care, who hides behind textbook cliches and outmoded panaceas while Canadians suffer.
At the same time we have his acolyte, the undistinguished minister responsible for housing, who trots around telling Canadians to lower their expectations, and to sit on orange crates. How could those expectations be lower while this gang remains in power?
This government has been overcome by an attack of unmitigated nationalism and Canadians are paying the penalty as the economy grinds to a halt. They have virtually transferred to the national field the policies advocated by Mr. Levesque and his friends at the provincial level. We even now have the incredible spectacle of the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox), in the name of his particular version of Canadian culture, threatening to tell Canadians what satellite programs they will be allowed to bring into this country. Next, they will be deciding what books Canadians can read.
So discredited is the minister's budget that rumours are flying in financial circles that it is about to be withdrawn and rewritten in its entirety. These rumours add to the prevailing uncertainty in money markets.
The budget has been rejected by the Ontario Liberals meeting in convention recently. They demanded a return of numerous incentives defined by the minister as "loopholes", including a restoration of the MURB program. That was one of the loopholes which the minister plugged, with the result that construction was frozen on some 20,000 housing units across the country. They demand tax-free interest on Small Business Development Bonds, tax deductibility for venture financing, and new incentives to entrepreneurs. The minister would do well to pay attention to these recommendations because, for once, the Liberal Party of Ontario appears to be in closer touch with what is going on in this country than this government is.
We have entered a phase of economic recession; homes are not being built, that is a fact; unemployment is spreading like
The Budget-Mr. Nielsen
a cancer across the country, and that is a fact; young people, those who have jobs, are being forced into debt by high mortgage rates, and that is a fact. Those are the miseries of this budget.
We are in this situation precisely because of the government's ill-advised and uninformed interventions in the economy, and because of the enormous spending by this government which has placed an insupportable burden on the economy as well as on the taxpayers.
Instead of cutting back on unnecessary expenditures, their solution is to increase taxes, squeeze the provinces and take more money out of the economy to finance their pet schemes, such as the $91 million loaned to a computer firm in Ottawa which subsequently went belly up, and the $6 million interest-free loan to an hotel promotion in Windsor, Ontario. These are the kinds of problems that get attention from this government. There has been a wholesale corruption of economic policy by the most blatant patronage considerations.
What is particularly disturbing is that, as the recession deepens and unemployment increases across the country, there is no sign of awareness by the minister or the government that Canadians are suffering. A recent report by Statistics Canada revealed that we have reached a zero growth situation in the economy, while inflation continues to increase without any signs of moderation. According to Statistics Canada, one of the major inflationary factors in the economy is the government's chauvinistic national energy policy, followed by the increased taxes on oil and gas, taxes which the Minister of Finance during the last election campaign said were going to be kept down as long as Canadians voted Liberal.
The budget is simply another example of the kind of authoritarian control which permeates every facet of this arrogant government's activities. What it is doing cannot be described as policies, for the benefit of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, any more than the aimless fluttering of moths around a flame can be described as policy. The flame is love of power and the arrogant assumption of a right to tell Canadians what they must do and how they must think to satisfy the criteria of these men on horseback.
They have alienated Quebec, bankrupted the economy, forced thousands into the soup kitchens, brought exploration and initiative to a standstill or forced it out of the country, and pushed the frontiers of achievement in this country back to the thirties. Every single major project in the energy field has been stifled and curtailed because of their unenlightened interference in the area of free choice. The country can no longer afford the luxury of this government.
It is not the budget alone which must go. The government which produced the budget has outlived its usefulness. That, sir, is why this evening we are taking the unprecedented course on the sixth and final day of a budget debate of requiring a standing vote. It is unprecedented, yes, for it is usually the custom on the sixth day to allow the budget to be adopted on division. But this, sir, is an unprecedented budget, unprecedented in the misery it is causing millions of Canadians. It is the worst 1 have seen since I have been here.

The Budget-Mr. J. R. Reid
I urge the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and the hon. member for York East to have the courage of their convictions and to do right by their constituents, along with any other of those 30 colleagues who met in caucus with the minister the other night, and vote against the continuation of this misery, if they are to do a service to their constituents.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say how much I enjoyed the speech by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). I thought he read it very well. I can recall the days before the hon. member for Yukon had the opportunity of being a cabinet minister and of spending some time in the ministry, where he usually had people to write his speeches for him, when he was able to stand in the House with a few notes written on the back of a cigar box and entertain us with witticisms we knew fell from the heart. Now what has happened? Because of the status to which he has now risen, he has fallen into the habit of having others write his speeches for him, as it was in the days when he was minister. I am one of those who regrets very much the lack of spontaneous wit with which the hon. member used to entertain the House. What we are getting now is written wit; written, I think, with a certain skill, but it certainly does not tumble from the lips the way it used to.
Now that the hon. member for Yukon has acceded to the position of House leader for the opposition, I know he would not want to accept a lesson in procedure from somebody as humble as myself. However, I did think it would be extremely useful to read to him the motion we are going to vote on tonight. The motion is found, of course, in the papers of the House of Commons and I will just read it, although the hon. member, I know, knows it full well. It says that the motion has been moved by Mr. MacEachen, seconded by Mr. Pinard:
That this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government.
It is on that motion, which we will be voting on at 9.45 p.m., that I will be casting my vote.
What I tell the House and the hon. gentleman is that in general I do approve the budgetary policy of the government. I say that I do have, as do many other members, reservations about the proposed changes in tax legislation contained in the budget. I think that is no secret. I think it is also fair to make clear, as the hon. member for Yukon fully understands, that we will not see what that legislative proposal is until probably after Christmas, at which time the legislation will go through the House in the usual way for tax legislation. There will be a choice given to the House, I hope, as to whether that legislation is dealt with on the floor of the House of Commons or in a standing committee. At that point, in one way or another it will go through three readings in the House of Commons. I will have the opportunity, as will other members, of speaking on the specific details of the tax policy, because it will only be then that they come into effect and become law.
It is on that basis that I have decided to support the budgetary policy of the government. I believe the budgetary
policy, as distinct from the tax policy, is reasonable under the circumstances.
The hon. member for Yukon has raised an interesting point, and that is the method by which we proceed in dealing with the budget in this House. It is clear from the examples of the last four or five budgets that the procedure we follow is inherently destructive. What happens when the budget is prepared? It is prepared by a very small number of officials in the tax policy section of the Department of Finance. They do not have the ability, as they have on almost any other item, to consult with other civil servants. Nor do they have the right and are not allowed to discuss tax policy with anybody outside the governmental system. So this is an extremely small group. Furthermore, to carry it to absurdity, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) traditionally does not discuss it with his colleagues in cabinet and usually the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is only informed after the budget is in the hands of the printer.
So we have this fundamentally important document developed in secrecy by an extremely small number of people, and consequently every Minister of Finance ultimately comes to the House saying that he made a mistake and had to change it. We have seen examples of this time and again with every Minister of Finance and it is accepted by the House as a normal part of the procedure. We have seen that when the Minister of Finance proposes tax policy changes, they are changed. If we study the tax policy changes of any Minister of Finance and then see what the final legislation says, we will find that almost every section is significantly changed.
The reason for that is simple. It is that this limited number of people simply cannot comprehend the totality of what the Canadian economy is all about. In many cases, the budgetary papers provide for a forum for the discussion of tax policy matters. That is another matter. In my judgment, it is separate from the question of over-all budgetary operations.
Why do we have all of this secrecy? I suspect there are two reasons. First, the British have it and ours is fundamentally a British system. Second, the Americans do not have it and for that reason it must be good if we have it.
It seems that we should be moving away from the tradition of secrecy and becoming more open by striking down the veil of secrecy, which does nothing more than encourage the debate of tax policy before we even have it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I might say that these excessive measures to impose budgetary secrecy are one of the main reasons why budgets do not very often meet the quality which we should demand and expect.
I have other suggestions for change. I think that once we eliminate the secrecy and open up the system, we must admit that there should be the possibility of releasing this information and the concepts that the minister is working on ahead of
December 8, 1981

time so that people will have an opportunity to comment on them, the same as is done for other legislative proposals. I also think that we have to eliminate retroactive legislation. I believe that that concept is foreign to parliamentary democracy. It is especially foreign to parliamentary democracy when we see that the retroactive legislation proposed by the minister is usually changed extensively before it takes its final form in law. As a consequence, we have three sets of laws occurring at one time. There is the law as it exists, the law as it exists in the words of the minister and the law as the Parliament of Canada will eventually develop it. Often there is a tremendous difference between those three forms of law.
The process as it now exists creates a great amount of uncertainty for business and for everyone in the economic community. Is strikes me that the time has come for us to eliminate this concept of retroactive legislation, but I would suggest that there be one exception, and that is that the minister have the authority to set rates when he brings down his budget. He can take the existing taxes and change the rates but should not have the authority to do the things which he has been doing, such as legislation being enacted retroactively. I think this is important and it should be one of the matters discussed in the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization.
I would also like to say that I am disappointed in the House leader because his long promised changes in procedures in the House of Commons have not yet appeared. This Parliament has been in session for nearly two years and I think this long delay should not be tolerated.
In examining the whole budgetary process, we must have regard to the way legislation is treated on the floor of the House. I think it is absurd that in this day and age our Standing Orders require that the budgetary bills be dealt with on the floor of the House of Commons. That requirement should be eliminated so that the legislation can be dealt with in committees so the ordinary citizens of Canada can appear before the committee and make their opinions known. It is not right that Canadians should have to make their views known through their Members of Parliament, who may or may not understand the complexity of their case. It is important to allow people to present their case directly and specifically to members sitting on the commmittee on matters as important as tax policies. That is a very important reform.
I could discuss the question of budgetary secrecy and the changes that I would like to see, but I will move now to the subject of budget basics. I generally approve of the basic thrust of the budget. For example, I think that the deficit has been far too large and that it is time we began to tackle it. It is time that the Minister of Finance and the Governor of the Bank of Canada sang the same tune, or at least sang in harmony. For the last number of years the Government of Canada and the Minister of Finance have followed one direction and the Governor of the Bank of Canada has gone the other way. I think the House should take note that for the first time they are at least trying to follow the same direction. That is a unique situation for which the Minister of Finance should
The Budget-Mr. J. R. Reid
be congratulated. It has not been an easy choice for him to make.
If hon. members were to review the speeches made during this debate, it would be evident that very few speeches have dealt with the budget itself. What we have heard from members on all sides of the House are pleas from individual groups of constituents who are being badly hurt by the current inflationary process. Those pleas should be made and listened to because there are casualties. However, if we look at what the solution would cost, the estimate is that if just the basic concerns were considered the government would be looking at an expenditure of a minimum of $20 million to protect the people who are caught up in the war against inflation. If we added all the expenditures that business has asked the government to make in one form or another on their behalf, we would be looking at another $20 million.
The fact of the matter is that at some point it must be decided how much revenue should be taken out of the system to spend on government programs. The government has decided to hold down the expenditures as much as possible in spite of the fact that it is carrying four massive spending programs in Canada at this time. The first of these massive spending programs is the subsidy to keep oil prices down. The amount of money the government has spent from 1974 to 1979 is $12 billion to subsidize the price of oil we import into Canada. That is a lot of money which comes out of the pocket of the average Canadian taxpayer. We are emerging from that program but the fact is that $12 billion has been spent from which there has been no real return.
The second large expenditure program is indexation. Most of our social expenditures have been indexed and, furthermore, we have indexed almost all of the revenue we get from individuals. Consequently, we have built into our spending approximately $2 million to $3 million every year, and the amount is increasing, to meet that indexation cost. This means that our expenditurs must go up to meet that cost. At the same time, we have built a decline into our revenue requirements because we have indexed the amount of revenue we are prepared to take. The cost of that indexation amounts to around $5 million a year. This is a massive spending program in itself. I think there is a general consensus in the House that we should continue that kind of program, but it costs a great deal of money.
The third spending program is-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is not spent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is money that is spent. It is money that the government must find somewhere in order to make those expenditures. For example, if the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is going to spend $1 billion on, say, the guaranteed income supplement program and that is indexed to the rate of inflation, the next year she not only has to find what she started off with but she also has to find the additional; so the consequence of that is that she

December 8, 1981
The Budget-Mr. J. R. Reid
must find, or the government must find, that amount of money every year. And let us remember that the government is not taking the inflationary quotient that is in the economy any more because we have indexed our revenues. The revenue goes down, expenditures go up and, in my judgment, that is a massive spending program.
The third spending program is, of course, the deficit. If we look at the amount of money it takes to service the deficit, we find that the deficit now takes up some 20 per cent of the budget of the federal government.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You made it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let us go back and take a look at that. Where does that deficit come from? I wanted to know where it came from, so I went to the research department of the Bank of Canada and asked where the Canadian deficit comes from. Does it come from indexation? Does it come from spending money on the oil subsidization program? No, I was told, it comes from the reduction in income taxes, sales taxes or corporation taxes which every Minister of Finance has put into his budget since 1974. Of course, they were behaving in a good Keynesian way. They were trying to pump up the economy. Pump, pump, pump every year and that made up 90 per cent of the deficit of $14 billion. If in fact that deficit came from that expenditure of money, lowering taxes means that eventually we have to pay for it, and we pay for it through the service of the national debt. We have done it so much that we have created a situation in which that is now the fastest growing spending program of the federal government.
When hon. members tell me that they do not want to have taxes raised but that they want to have expenditures increased substantially to look after the people who are being hurt, I have to ask hon. members where the money comes from. Do we go back to the market and borrow more, squeeze out the private borrower and raise interest rates by competitive action? Do we raise taxes to try to pay if off and to control it? Or do we ask the Bank of Canada to start printing money and increase our inflation rate? I know of no other way that the Government of Canada can raise money than by those ways, and I certainly would like hon. members who come to the House of Commons to plead the case of their afflicted constituents to tell us where we are to get the money and how it should be expended.
We have a real problem in this country, and that is what this budget is all about. It is one of the first budgets I can recall which really tries to deal with the over-all financial state of the Canadian government and tries to relate it to what the Bank of Canada is doing and to Canada's position in the world. I think the Minister of Finance deserves a great deal of credit for that. I would have been happier with what the Minister of Finance had done had we had a debate on that subject in this budget debate, but if hon. members look at the speeches which have been made during this debate, they will find that the number of people who have tried to address this very difficult question is indeed very small. I say to the hon. member for Yukon that I am going to vote for this budget
because it tries to address the real questions in the Canadian economy.
I want to quote an economist under whose regime we are now living. Perhaps I might better say whose regime we are leaving.
-if (my) ideas are correct... it would be a mistake, I predict to dispute their potency over a period of time ... the ideas of economists and political philosophers, both when they are right and when they are wrong, are more powerful than is commonly understood. Indeed, the world is ruled by little else. Practical men, who believe themselves to be quite exempt from any intellectual influences, are usually the slaves of some defunct economist. Madmen in authority, who hear voices in the air, are distilling their frenzy from some academic scribbler of a few years back. I am sure that the power of vested interests is vastly exaggerated compared with the encroachment of ideas. Not, indeed, immediately, but after a certain interval; for in the field of economics and political philosophy there are not many who are influenced by new theories after they are twenty-five or thirty years of age, so that the ideas which civil servants and politicians and even agitators apply to current events are not likely to be the newest. But sooner or later, it is ideas, not vested interests, which are dangerous for good or evil.
For hon. members who are curious as to who wrote that, it was John Maynard Keynes in the concluding page of "The General Theory".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What year?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was 1936.
One of the things which concerns us is that we seem to have come to the end of the Keynesian period. The concept of high inflation combined with high unemployment is something which is not possible under Keynesian theory. It certainly was not predicted, and certainly Keynesians have no idea how to deal with it. It may well be that the Keynesian theory, which was developed at a different time and in a different place and which was implemented by governments more or less after the Second World War, is like those sub-atomic particles which physicists study and which physicists have said that in the act of studying them, you change them.
It may be that the implementation of Lord Keynes' theory has actually changed the economy so that the theory itself no longer applies to the economy which has been created as a result of the application of that theory. I do not know. I am not an economist. I am not a trained economist, but I do know that if Lord Keynes is correct about the scribblings of madmen which are followed by politicians, civil servants and business leaders, if he is correct that the theory will be important to these people because it gets into the environment in which people move and act, and if it is true that we have come to the end of that theory, what theory do we follow when we come to framing our budgetary policies? What theory do we follow when, in our own individual lives, we come to predicting the future and making our own personal investments? If we are in the corporate sector, how do we make the same kinds of judgments about the money that is saved by ordinary people? If we do not have a road map and if we do not know where we are, how can we determine where we want to go?
I think the real dilemma right now is that there is no road map that applies. There is no consensus in economic theory in North America. Having returned from a month in Europe
December 8, 1981

where I had the opportunity to talk with a great many leading politicians and civil servants about the problems their economies in the Common Market were facing, I can tell hon. members that they also have no road map at all. If we examine what is going on in the world, we will see that each country has taken a different tack. The countries of the world have tried different theories, and at the present time the world is a laboratory of conflicting economic theory being put into practice. All of us in the OECD countries are suffering from the same malaise. We are all suffering from high unemployment, high interest rates and a lack of markets, and it seems to me that if in fact these conditions of the disease are not unique to Canada but are found in almost every other country, the best we can do is try to analyse our own set of circumstances and cut our cloth according to those circumstances. We should be examining with a great deal of care what is going on in other countries so that we can see perhaps more of the forest and less of the trees, where some of the paths go and avoid going down some of the dead-end alleys.
It strikes me that we have not yet begun that part of the exercise in Canada because the debates up until now show that this has been a subject most hon. members have avoided like the plague. I admit that I have no answers, but I do say that the Minister of Finance is about the only politician in this country who has attempted to grapple with these questions and to take the Canadian economy, and particularly the financial status of the Government of Canada, and try to put it on a new track and combine what is going on in the operations of the Government of Canada with those of the Bank of Canada. As I said, this is the first time in a long time that a Minister of Finance and the Governor of the Bank of Canada have been going down the same path. While it may not lead us to the promised land, Mr. Speaker, it is a lot better than to have them go in opposite directions. On that basis, it is a decision which impresses me enough that I can happily vote for the budget, with no regret.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with considerable care and attention to the remarks made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid). The hon. member went into the question of economic theory, a matter that I shall return to in the last couple of minutes of what I have to say.
One of the great things about budgets is that they tell the truth. Whether a budget is a family budget, a national budget, a provincial budget or a municipal budget, budgets do a couple of things. First of all, it tells exactly where one is in relation to the numbers one has to work with; it tells the people in a family or in a nation what kind of vision the government might have, what kind of philosophy operates behind the budget.
Unfortunately, in the last number of years it has been very difficult for people to understand budgets. Budgets have become incredibly complicated. If I may, Mr. Speaker, let me read one quote which I had from the now President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) when he made a comment
The Budget-Mr. Crombie
with respect to what had recently happened to budgets. He said that budgets had now taken up more time and more energy by accountants and lawyers than it would have taken had they been involved in some productive labour-that is the final part of the quote. Because, indeed, it is difficult for ordinary individual taxpayers to understand how they are being affected by the budget. It is even more complicated for people in small and medium-sized businesses to understand what indeed is happening to them.
The other night the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) rose in his place and said: "I have for you a budget which does three things; it is going to give restraint"-everyone is in favour of restraint-"it is going to offer equity"-everyone is in favour of fairness-"it is going to offer recovery"-we are all desperately seeking recovery, Mr. Speaker. When he said those things, most people said, that is right, that is what we want. Those honeyed words of "restraint", "equity" and "recovery" were just what everyone wanted to hear. That is why the initial response to the budget in the newspapers, on radio and television was something like "a neutral budget". One newspaper was quoted as stating that. Someone else called it "a stand pat budget". Another said "housekeeping".
The fact of the matter is that initially everyone listened not to the budget but to the words about the budget. They did not listen to the song but to the singer. Every time one does that, one tends to lose the reality of what is happening. Indeed, many people of this country began to be seduced into saying: "Gee, I guess it is all right". That was until, of course, they were able to read more, listen more, think more, and then the whole thing began to unravel before their very eyes. Because it was a budget not of any large slash; it was a budget of one thousands cuts. The cuts were not in the budget, but it affected increasingly more and more people. As those little circles began to go towards the shore, hon. members of the House, journalists, the media and other people who observed the scene began to get the effects of those ripples. The gathering storm about this budget got bigger and bigger and bigger. It will not go away, Mr. Speaker. I should like to explain to the Chair and to the House why I believe the gathering storm hovering over the Minister of Finance and hovering over this country will not go away. The demand for the revision of the budget will increase daily. It is increasing now and it will increase in the future.
Let me look, first of all, at the question of equity. Indeed, when the Minister of Finance read the budget speech, he spent most of his time on equity. He had little to say about restraint, and even less to say about recovery. He spent most of his time on equity, because he knows that Canadians are instinctively fair-minded people who like to have fair treatment. They like to have fair treatment for themselves and they like to have fair treatment for other Canadians.
Let us look at the second principle in the budget, equity. Whom does this budget favour? Where is the equity? For whom does that equity flow in this budget? Is it fair, Mr. Speaker, to home owners? There are 1.2 million home owners who will renegotiate their mortgages over the next few months

December 8, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Crombie
at interest rates which are not only unacceptable but impossible for them to manage on the money they earn. The minister responsible for housing, who is present in the House, knows that from a CMHC report from his officials. CMHC predicts that 40,000 Canadians will lose their homes in the next short while. Is that the fairness that is supposed to be in the budget? Is that the equity, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I want facts.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member wants facts, Mr. Speaker. If the hon. member will allow me the short time I am allowed, and if he takes notes, he will have them. The hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) should take some notes, because there are people in his constituency who would like to know what those facts are. They know the facts that are affecting them. For example, look at renters, Mr. Speaker. There is no choice now in this country as to whether or not one will rent an apartment or a home as opposed to owning a home. The vacancy rate in this country is now at 0.3. According to the budget of the Minister of Finance in 1983 the vacancy rate will approach zero. That is a fact, I say to the hon. member for Ottawa Centre. If one were to examine the budget, there is no choice any more for renters in this country. We are supposed to build 90,000 new rental units to keep up with the demand we already have. At best, if one were to use the figures to the best of their ability, the budget offers 15,000. That is not fair.
I spent yesterday in All Saints Church in downtown Toronto. It is now called the "Church of last resort". Every hostel space in Toronto now has one and a half claims on it. There are 50 per cent more people looking for space than we have available in hostels alone. Is that fair?
What about the unemployed? Maybe they see that the equity comes to the unemployed in this budget. There are almost one million people on record looking for work in this country. That is 8.2 per cent of the work force, including 62,000 people in the residential construction industry alone. Is it fair to them? The unemployment rate for native people in this country is 35 per cent to 75 per cent. Is it fair to them?
Forty-one per cent of the women in this country who are sole supporters for their families live below the Stats Canada poverty line. Is that fair? Is that what the government means by "fair"? Maybe it is fair to the young people, I say to the hon. member for Ottawa Centre. Maybe that is what the hon. member means. The unemployment rate for young people between the ages of 15 and 24 is 14.1 per cent. Every time one reads the unemployment figures, Mr. Speaker, one should remember that 44 per cent of those figures represents people between the ages of 15 and 24. That is not fair.
Is the government doing anything about job creation in this budget? There is not one new initiative in the budget with regard to job creation. Out of all of the pages in the whole of the budget, there is only one page that deals with human resource development. They did not even use the entire page. It called for a comprehensive review of job creation in the 1980s. It is now almost 1982. The time for job creation for the 1980s was in the 1970s, so that young people would have a
chance. Is there any opportunity for growth in our educational institutions to train young people in technical and technological fields? The answer is no. The government is cutting back $5.7 billion over the next five years in grants to educational institutions which engage in technical and technological education. Is that fair? Is that what the government means by fair.
Is it equity? For whom is it equity? Is it equity for small and medium-sized businesses? Do they remember small and medium-sized businesses? First, small and medium-sized businesses create the majority of new jobs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is the same speech you have given for the last number of years. Get down to the details.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Second, they make a major contribution to growth in the country through technological innovation. Third, all these businesses are technologically and research intensive. I have mentioned these things about small and medium-sized businesses because the clack over there who keep yelling will pay for it dearly when they meet with their constituents. They know this from their own mail and telephone calls. The government, through this budget, dealt a body blow to small and medium-sized businesses from which they may never recover for years to come. This is why the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, which represents 63,000 businesses in the country, declared war on the government, on the budget and on the minister. The federation did this because it knew that the budget offered absolutely no opportunity for investment, which creates jobs.
Perhaps it is fair to senior citizens. One in every three people over the age of 65 lives below the Statistics Canada poverty line; 350,000 women over the age of 65 live below the poverty line. Of those between the ages of 55 and 64, 39.4 per cent live below the poverty line; between the ages of 65 and 69, 34.6 per cent; over the age of 70, 48 per cent. I notice the hon. member for Ottawa Centre is not paying any attention to these facts. The reason I mention senior citizens is because absolutely no relief was promised them in the budget. Worse, the government has prated about the necessity of pension plans in the private sector being better so that they serve more Canadians. The budget taxed registered retirement savings plans and life insurance policies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is untrue and you know it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what the budget did to people who have worked hard for decades to save money and put it away on a monthly basis against their old age. The government decided to take as much of it as it could. Hon. members opposite do not like to hear this because they know it is the truth.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is totally false.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What about equity and recovery? The budget is an unmitigated and uncovered attack on incentive, individual effort and creative spirit.
December 8, 1981

The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) was interested in how we were to get new money. He was very interested and concerned about the theory of getting money to pay for things. One theory which has always worked is to ensure that those who want to invest and to create jobs are allowed to do it. It is not a government budget which creates wealth. Is is the people of the country who create wealth, and it is the budget which is holding them back. That is how they get money for programs.
The gathering storm will continue because there is a smell of tragedy about the budget. People really know this down deep. It said to people: "Remember how you used to think you could get ahead? Forget it. Remember how you used to think there were chances and opportunities? Forget those."
The budget needs to be revised. Indeed I predict, despite what the clack says, that the Minister of Finance will revise the budget. Because he must revise it, and he must listen to the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. The federation set out the following rather neatly in the newspaper today:
The MacEachen budget is not what it seems to be. It is a sly, devious document that nearly fooled us all.
Absolutely, and this is why the minister will change the budget. Hon. members opposite who do not want to listen to the truth will have to find something else to say, because the people of the country will not stand for a budget which locks their future behind doors.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity this afternoon to speak in the budget debate. First I wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on his choice of the three important themes that form the basis of his budget: restraint, equity and economic renewal. A number of the budget's provisions, including tax relief for owners of small businesses and farmers who are severely affected by interest rates, are very important to thousands of my constituents. Many low-income families in my riding will benefit from tax reductions as a result of a tax rebate. This special rebate now stands at 9 per cent of income tax, with a minimum of $200 and a maximum of $500. From now on, it will be set at $200 for all taxpayers, while married taxpayers will be able to claim $200 more for their dependent spouse. Since indexing of personal income has been maintained, personal exemptions for a family of four will be raised from $7,230 to $8,110 next year, while the child tax credit will increase from $261 to $293 per child, as a result of indexing and the budget measures.
The average family of four will be able to earn about $15,000 in 1982 without paying income tax to the government of Canada. These measures, and others I shall be mentioning later in my speech, should have a beneficial effect in my riding. I could of course spend my allotted time on subjects of national interest only, but I prefer to use half for these and
The Budget-Mr. Lefebvre
half for issues that are directly of interest to my constituents. The first half of my speech will concern important issues in my riding. One of these is the increasing involvement of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in my riding of Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle. The department's financial contribution will play a very important role in boosting the region's economy. Under the Canada-Quebec subsidiary agreement on development of tourism, the Minister of DREE (Mr. De Bane) suggested to his Quebec counterpart last July that the scope of the agreement could be enlarged to include a new program to support the development of international standard ski resorts, such as Mont Sainte-Marie which is going to be one of the most important resorts of its kind in Canada.
This measure will involve expenditures totalling $13 million, 60 per cent of which is to be paid by the Canadian government and 40 per cent by the government of the province of Quebec. Thus, DREE's contribution under this agreement will be $7.8 million. Mont Sainte-Marie will be the first activity supported under this component of the agreement. The government of Canada is willing to participate financially in developing this fantastic resort location. I fail to understand why the government of Quebec has not yet made its position clear, and in so doing is postponing indefinitely an important project in a region that urgently needs jobs. DREE is also involved in road construction in the region. For instance, construction of the Maniwaki-Temiscamingue highway is being financed 60 per cent by the government of Canada, which is paying $15 million of the total cost of $25 million, while the remaining $10 million is to be paid by the province of Quebec. This permanent highway linking Maniwaki to Temiscamingue is part of the Canada-Quebec subsidiary agreement on forestry development. This access road to forest resources in the area will provide a more rational development of the huge hardwood and softwood lots while promoting tourism.
Under the Canada-Quebec agreement on forest development, another road which will also give access to forest resources and promote tourist development will connect with the Maniwaki-Temiscamingue highway in the Pontiac at Lake Nilgault. The section under construction extends from the Bois-Franc Road at Fort-Coulonge to Lake Jim. According to the agreement signed between the two levels of government and the lumber companies E. B. Eddy and Consolidated Bathurst, 50 per cent of the cost will be paid by the governments and 50 per cent by the companies involved. Under an auxiliary agreement on major roads, expenditures estimated at $36 million are earmarked for the reconstruction of highway 117 from St-Jovite in the Laurentians to Louvincourt in the Abitibi. This highway goes through Mont-Laurier in the north of the Gatineau constituency near Grand-Remous. The federal contribution is $21,600,000 and that of Quebec $14,400,000.
Mr. Speaker, I had suggested some time ago that the Government of Canada sponsor an information day in the Pontiac area of my constituency. The Pontiac Businessmen

December 8, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Lefebvre
Association agreed to sponsor it itself and it was effectively held last March. On that occasion, four federal departments sent representatives to explain their programs and policies to businessmen and others. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane) attended the closing ceremony of the information day and this was much appreciated by the audience. This event gave rise to substantial achievements, since DREE decided to undertake a study on the economic revival of the Pontiac. This study has now been completed and I am convinced that it will help greatly to find the necessary solutions to promote the rational development of the Pontiac area of this large constituency.
Tomorrow night, Mr. Speaker, together with officials of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and some Quebec government representatives, I will take part in Campbells Bay in a luncheon sponsored once again by the Pontiac Businessmen Association. I hope that during the discussions that will follow, we will be able to set in motion an action plan for the citizens of Pontiac. Again recently, the representatives of the City of Maniwaki and the Upper Gatineau Development Association appeared before the Subcommittee on Regional Economic Expansion at the hearings it held in Sherbrooke and submitted briefs in which they asked DREE to get involved more directly in the economic revival of the Upper Gatineau Valley. The DREE study group will meet shortly to consider the feasability of sponsoring a study on the economic renewal of the Upper Gatineau Valley. I certainly hope, following the studies carried out in Pontiac and those which are very likely to be carried out in the Upper Gatineau Valley, that DREE will decide to make this a designated area. DREE would thus be able to get involved unilaterally and directly in the economic renewal of this constituency, without having to wait for Quebec's requests which are sometimes very long in coming.
Mr. Speaker, another very interesting program for the constituency is that initiated on November 3 by the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission. The first Local Economic Development Assistance Agency-or ADEL as it is known in Quebec-was officially inaugurated on that day in Maniwaki. This new organization, known as the LEDA Agency of Upper Gatineau, obtained a grant of $250,000 for its first year of operation. Out of this, some $150,000 will be used to stimulate employment, and the remaining $100,000 will pay the costs of technical and administrative assistance to businesses. The financial involvement of the agency in the projects it will receive will be through loans or the purchase of shares, up to a maximum of $25,000 per business. Up to now, only twelve such agencies have been established throughout Canada. The creation of this LEDA Agency in the Upper Gatineau Valley should continue to create new jobs, thereby contributing to the fight against unemployment which is an all-permeating cancer in this region. I hope that in the near future two other areas of the constituency, namely, Pontiac and Labelle, will get LEDA agencies of their own. In order to
encourage job creation, the Government of Canada has granted, through the Department of Employment and Immigration, a $99,000 subsidy to the Societe cooperative d'action et d'ini-tiative municipale de Notre-Dame-de-Pontmain under a LEAP project. This subsidy has made possible the creation of 5 jobs over a one year period. During this planning stage, the employees of the project will look into the feasibility of setting up a plant for manufacturing chip-wood planks.
Once the planning stage is over and if the study proves that such a project would be profitable and viable, the promoters might be given additional grants to carry it out. Mr. Speaker, over the past five years the government of Canada through the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation, has invested in excess of $11 million to repair, modernize and alter hundreds of houses in the various municipalities of the riding. At least a third of those $11 million were in the form of direct grants and the balance was made up of long term loans at very attractive prime rates. Besides making it possible for the owners of those houses to live in better conditions, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program did create new jobs while at the same time encouraging local building material dealers.
Mr. Speaker, we should note as well the importance of all the other programs implemented by the government of Canada in the housing area, such as the low-rental houses which were built in a number of municipalities in the riding, and financed mostly by the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation, as well as homes for senior citizens, the Neighbourhood Improvement Program in the urban centres of Maniwaki and Mont-Laurier, and the Community Services Contribution Program. Mr. Speaker, the farmers in my riding are among the most active in Canada. Our beef producers rank first in Quebec since they account for more than one third of the total production of the province.
Just recently I had the opportunity to meet here in Ottawa with a representative group of feed lot operators from Pontiac.
