Also present were officials from the Farm Credit Corporation, the small business secretariat and Agriculture Canada, including an adviser from the minister's office and representatives of two banks. These beef producers explained the reasons they are encountering very grave financial difficulties. The discussion explored ways by which the measures announced in the budget could be quickly implemented in order to help these producers. It was agreed that decisions were needed in the coming weeks in order for measures to be effective.
I support these initiatives and trust that the solutions can be found very quickly.

I also had an opportunity to meet the spokesmen for the dairy producers of my riding who told me about their worries concerning the financial difficulties they are facing, as are all Canadians. They are impatiently awaiting the announcement

which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) will be making about the forthcoming dairy year as soon as the special study now under way is received and analysed. Dairy production is a major component of the economy of our area and I echo the wishes of the producers that the policy will be based on hard facts, that it will be a fair policy which will continue to provide producers with an adequate income which will give them a standard of living to match their work load and their productivity. I am pleased to note that in his budget the Minister of Finance kept the farmers in mind, particularly those whose financial situation is rather shaky. They could benefit from special loans from the Farm Credit Corporation whose interest rates are lower by as much as five percentage points, which would bring current rates of 16.75 per cent down to 11.75 per cent. Thus they will henceforth be eligible under the Small Business Development Bond program. Mr. Speaker, ever since the "Petit train du Nord" has been discontinued, some 5,000 electors, mostly in my riding, have made representations and four very specific recommendations which I have been glad to support.
These recommendations were basically as follows: That the railway be maintained and that the freight train remain in operation, that the "little train" occasionally, as for special events, go up to Mont-Laurier, that the opportunity of providing an electric train service in the region be studied, and that the Mont-Laurier station be declared a heritage building. Last Sunday, I also attended a public meeting on that same issue in Mont-Laurier with about a hundred people concerned about the future of the rail service between Montreal and Mont-Laurier. We discussed these four recommendations. During the meeting, I was able to discuss with those people for three or four hours and trade views and ideas with them on this issue.
With respect to urea formaldehyde foam insulation, 1 am fully aware that this might inconvenience some homeowners of my riding as well as elsewhere in the country, but I agree with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs that we must await the results of the tests conducted throughout the country so that the action that will be decided upon is based on the recommendations and findings of the commission of inquiry. I hope that the study will be completed as quickly as possible and that the action taken is fair for all concerned.
Another important issue in my riding, Mr. Speaker, is Camp Gatineau. For several years and especially in the last weeks I have spared no effort to avoid the closing of the camp. The camp is located within Gatineau park, on NCC land, and accommodates every year several hundred mentally handicapped people from Quebec, most of whom come from outside the Ottawa Valley. I was quite happy, especially in this international year of the disabled, to hear the Minister of DREE announce that his department was immediately going to approach the Quebec government so that the Camp Gatineau renewal project and the $450,000 required, would be included in the Quebec-Canada subsidiary agreement on tour-
The Budget-Mr. Lefebvre
ism development in order to achieve the objectives of this camp for the handicapped.
In view of all the facts that I have so far highlighted in my remarks, you will no doubt have realized by now, Mr. Speaker, that I am speaking for this region. That is indeed the case because I am fully aware of the tremendous efforts made up to now in order to improve the standard of living of my constituents. But increased efforts and considerable help will be needed in order to stimulate the economy of the region and thus encourage job creation and check unemployment which is endemic in this riding. The residents of the area want stable and permanent jobs. They are grateful for the economic benefits as well as for the many temporary jobs created by community development projects, as well as for the services and equipment made available to them. However, with a budget of $1.8 million for this winter, we all know that these are only temporary jobs and these people are concerned about the future because they hope to find permanent jobs in the area, particularly in the riding of Pontiac-Papineau-Labelle, in order to stop the flow of people leaving for more promising areas.

I would now like to speak as the former chairman of the Special Committee on Alternative Energy and Oil Substitution which was established on May 23, 1980. I am pleased that the budget contains measures dealing with energy. This seven-man, all-party special committee was given a mandate to explore and report upon new energy sources, technologies and fuels of potential interest to Canada, with particular regard to the technical and economic feasibility of their introduction. One year of intensive study and research was needed before the committee was able to arrive at conclusions and make its recommendations.
On the basis of the array of information, opinion and first-hand observation, the committee tabled a remarkable document containing 65 specific recommendations. The report looks ahead 50 years and foresees a fundamentally altered energy system in Canada.

Hydro-electric generation will continue to increase until our whole hydraulic potential has been nearly exhausted, probably early in the forthcoming century. The committee has found low-heads of water of growing interest and, in particular, small generating stations; it would appear that the technology involved is also ready to be exported. Considering Canada's conventional energy infrastructure and its evolution, how can alternative energy sources which seem so promising be integrated into it? The solution becomes more obvious when one turns the question around and looks at the energy markets in need of supplies. From that point of view, the advantages of hydrogen as a fuel or energy currency become obvious. [English]
In line with one of the recommendations contained in the report, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
December 8, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Lefebvre
Lalonde) announced in July that the federal government will increase funds for energy research and development by $35 million. The increased funds will provide more technical support for the following policy priorities which were established in the National Energy Program: developing new liquid fuel alternatives to gasoline; increasing the efficiency of energy use in all sectors of the economy; developing environmentally acceptable alternatives to oil and gas; and ensuring the continuing development of conventional energy for the benefit of all Canadians.
[ Translation]
The study made by the committee has enabled us to discover that converting our conventional energy infrastructure is quite a challenge especially because of its magnitude, its complexity and the massive investments it involves. If we are aiming at such a restructuring, then, according to the committee, the hard facts of life will have to be faced. We shall have to put our resources to other uses, provoking in all likelihood the protests of the affected sectors of industry. We shall have to expect new attitudes and new technologies, both of which will require considerable time. The public will have to recognize the need to change and adapt to new energy systems. In addition, as the elected representatives of the people usually know very little about technology, one wonders who in fact will advocate the change. Finally, it is becoming increasingly difficult to make radical decisions in today's society.
The members also considered it essential to formulate their recommendations in view of a guiding philosophy. Consequently the report lays out principles or concerns which the committee felt very strongly should form the foundation for domestic energy planning. These policy elements are energy conservation, progressively greater reliance on sustainable energy sources, minimal environmental disruption, greater diversity in Canada's energy mix, recognition of regional differences in energy resources and requirements, acknowledgment of strategic concerns, and consideration of the social implications of altering our nation's energy system.

At first glance, one might wonder at finding conservation under the heading "Alternative Energy Sources, Currencies and Technologies". But the committee was drawn to the conclusion that conservation should be looked upon as a source of energy, and an important one at that for Canada, especially because we have never been particularly concerned about energy efficiency in the past. Energy has always come cheap in Canada and that explains why our economy has evolved in such a way that we now use more energy per dollar of gross national product than any other industrialized country in the world. Paradoxically, this means that while our wasteful consumer habits of the past might have been regrettable, we now have a major energy source available because of conservation,
which source can be used more easily and more economically than any other existing resource. By reducing demand, we increase the relative value of existing energy supplies. Many witnesses who appeared before the committee stated that conservation should be the starting point of any alternative energy strategy, and we fully agree. We can view conservation as a reduced utilization of a resource in the short term to have more available in the long term.
The members of the committee would like all housing financed by the Canadian government to be built in accordance with conservation principles and to use passive solar heating to show the benefits of such systems. Energy performance standards should be incorporated into the National Building Code to promote innovation and conservation in building concepts. Both commercial and residential buildings should make use of lighting systems which do not waste electricity. Mr. Speaker, as those who spoke before me, I shall conclude my comments in a few moments so that other members can have an opportunity to speak as the debate will end this evening. In closing, I would simply like to say that I shall come back to the issue of new and renewable energy sources in the future. I think that the committee has tabled a very important report. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has already announced several initiatives based on our recommendations and I am convinced that there will be more in the future. I think that this report can be very important for our energy future in Canada because its recommendations can not only help Canada to become self-sufficient in oil supplies, but will also contribute to the creation of thousands of jobs in Canada in export industries thanks to new technologies developed in this country. Mr. Speaker, I believe that during these few minutes, I have been able to outline vitally important issues for the future of my constituents and for the energy future of Canada in general.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank you for giving me this opportunity to comment on a budget that many people have described as inadequate under the present circumstances, both as it affects my province and as it affects the entire country.
This evening we are being asked to support a budget that should normally be in tune with the present economic conditions. We are being asked to support a document that is absolutely devastating for the entire Canadian economy, a document that is totally unacceptable, and that, according to thousands of Canadians, will leave Canada in an economic quagmire. I feel it is also important to point out that in other speeches I have heard, especially from the government benches, the minister has been approached with a number of suggestions, a fact that in itself should be ample proof of the inadequacy of this budget vis-a-vis the problems facing the people in their ridings.
December 8, 1981

It is also interesting to note, Mr. Speaker, and I think Canadians will realize this in the medium term and I hope even sooner, that the budgets we have had in the last fifteen years have been remarkable for their ineptness and that they have been unable to provide a sufficient stimulus to the Canadian economy. And going back a little over the past fifteen years, we realize that things are going from bad to worse, and that despite the projections our Ministers of Finance have given us over the last fifteen years, no solution has been found, nor has it been possible to realize this famous equity which the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) has said he would make a reality. My colleague from Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) proved earlier that the commitments made by the Minister of Finance and his concept of equity, as presented in the budget, will be impossible to realize. In his speech, the member for Rosedale proved time and time again that the budget is unfair to thousands of Canadians. In my riding, as in the rest of Canada, Mr. Speaker, farmers and workers are very concerned.
From what has been said by members from every part of Canada, it is clear that the Canadian people are anxious, they are concerned and cannot be sure what the future holds in store, and they will certainly find no reassurances in the measures contained in this budget, and, quite frankly and objectively, these measures are certainly not going to set the minister and his government the confidence he is seeking from the House. I know perfectly well, Mr. Speaker, that the members on the government benches will have to support the budget, with probably more reservations than ever before. Those members are well aware that farmers are not getting what they need from this budget, that workers did not get what they were seeking, that homeowners will have to wait and spend another winter in an untenable position, that tenants will not get what they were promised and so on for thousands of Canadians. The members on the government benches are very familiar with the reactions of the business world and various organizations and sectors. But the system being what it is, they will have to support the Minister of Finance and hope and pray.
Earlier, I heard some comments from hon. members who were quite rightly seeking from the minister a number of corrective measures to remedy the omission or absence of adequate measures in the budget. Figures have been given and statistics have been put before the House, but the fact remains that the Canadian people not only have a right to be concerned, they will also have to remain in a limbo of uncertainty as a result of a totally inadequate budget. During question period the minister will try, as he has on other occasions, to make Canadians believe that with his budget cuts, Canada will get back on the road to prosperity, and that is just not true! I feel that Canadians are at least entitled to know the truth. The situation is alarming, and the economic policies that have been
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
presented by the present government during the last fifteen years have brought Canada to the brink of bankruptcy. Members opposite will consider this an exaggeration, but this is the situation which we are now facing, and thousands of Canadians, thousands of unemployed, are concerned about the absence of appropriate action.
Some will ask me if I have the solution myself. Since Canada has been left to drift for so long, it is of course impossible to find a miraculous solution in 24 hours. This would be unthinkable and it is impossible to correct such a situation immediately, but it is important for Canadians to recognize that it is this Liberal government which is responsible for that kind of brinkmanship. This is the situation. Mr. Speaker, no government member and no minister can assure Canadians that the situation will improve in the short term. This situation has been brought about by the marked incompetence of past ministers of finance and the members who have supported them in the last 15 years.
I am thinking especially about the farmers and the homeowners. The absence of appropriate action in the areas of housing and the building industry has created the dilemna now facing the country. The minister responsible for housing has demonstrated that he can no longer cope. He was unable to convince the Minister of Finance to provide sufficient funds to meet the demand. Because of this, the budget does not promote recovery of the building industry, which has been frozen for 18 months, or nearly two years, creating unemployment and putting Canadians in a terrible situation. The budget does not meet housing needs, and every member of the House realizes it.

speechtext:
They say that it is untrue. It is incredible, Mr. Speaker! The budget does not meet our needs and those who want to be honest will have to recognize it. This lack of policy in the field of construction and housing has been costly for Canadians. And I could say the same about agriculture. Nearly every member has met with farmers from my constituency and elsewhere and representatives of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the UPA in Quebec, and so on recently. Farmers are very concerned about the lack of action of the government and the minister concerning dairy policies, for instance. The minister has not applied the indexing formula to dairy producers, which he should normally have done in August. The minister has not announced his five-year plan as he was supposed to do last April, and the Minister of Finance has not provided the necessary funds for the Farm Credit Corporation. Moreover, dairy producers still do not know what to expect and they fear that the subsidies on dairy products will be abolished or reduced.
I think that all the members of this House whose constituency includes dairy producers want the minister to announce his policies as soon as possible, before January 1. I hope that he

December 8, 1981
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
will do so and I take this opportunity to appeal to the Minister of Agriculture, who is responsible for a very important industry, at least in my province and also in Ontario, since the dairy industry is centralized in those two provinces. I believe that it is important for the Minister of Agriculture to make these announcements as soon as possible, to ensure dairy producers that the subsidies will be maintained and to apply the indexing formula based on production costs.
Moreover, as farmers already have told the Minister of Finance, this budget does not respond to the financial needs of the farming community, and this scarcity of funds may force our agriculture into stagnation as it did with the construction industry, a tremendously important industry, and this in turn will mean increased unemployment. The budget does not provide for these two areas, absolutely not, and this is affecting thousands of Canadians because there is no resumption of activity in the building industry and a lack of funds to maintain and promote agriculture.
An hon. member referred earlier to the victims of urea-formaldehyde foam insulation. The government has remained absolutely mute on this. They felt that there was no need to provide funds to help those victims, and this is serious in my view. We are aware that thousands of Canadians are faced with that problem. We are aware that thousands of homeowners have problems not only with their mortgage costs but also with toxic foam insulation. The government or the responsible minister have not yet seen fit to recommend a special fund to help the victims clean up those homes, at a cost of thousands of dollars. I know perfectly well that the government, aware of the scope of that problem, does not dare get involved because this will prove too costly. Can you imagine leaving the whole burden with the home owners? The minister involved suggests that when the review is completed, he will see to it that the people responsible pay the costs.
It seems to me that if the minister had any sense of responsibility, he would accept recommending to Treasury Board that a special fund be established to help the victims. After such an investigation, it will be much easier for the government to recoup the expenses from the responsible parties. For the time being the government, through the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) denies any responsibility in the matter. Let the investigation follow its course. But what if the government is responsible? Government actions lead us to wonder about its own responsibility. Anyway, it has a moral obligation because this is a social problem, and I submit that the government should now help the victims with something more than a promise of an investigation or of certain services.
I would also like to refer briefly to the amazing discovery made by the Minister of Finance. All of a sudden, the Minister of Finance, in his budget, has mentioned loopholes. He was going to recoup thousands of dollars, if not millions, from those loopholes. Big joke, Mr. Speaker! Because those provisions, those loopholes were developed and provided for by the
same government. These so-called tax incentives were designed to stimulate the Canadian economy. That selfsame government had allowed some Canadians tax relief in conjunction with the purchase of goods and services and in other ways. But what that government had considered as incentives for years, the minister now sees in a different light. All of a sudden he says: I have made the discovery of the century. I shall recover billions of tax dollars and sneakily trap the Canadian to whom those advantages were offered. Because in fact Canadians had been encouraged to avail themselves of those loopholes. Today, these are plugged up without notice. We know hundreds of Canadians will have problems as a result of that radical step.
I have no quarrel with changing tax measures occasionally, it has to be done. But let no one have me believe that suddenly the minister grows vigilant when taking away what Canadians were granted a few years earlier. And above all, let no one claim that those Canadians were bad citizens because they availed themselves of those loopholes. Those people have never intended to cheat Revenue Canada, not at all! They simply used what measures the government had made available which, I say it again, were considered as relief and incentives. The government may have had a change of heart because of circumstances. Still, I wish it had kept its word and honoured its long-term commitments which benefit many Canadians, even if it did have to put an end to them in due course. I think it is nothing but sheer hypocrisy, Mr. Speaker, and certainly no proof of outstanding quality, when the Minister of Finance gives the impression that he has found something really exceptional.
Two or three times, and perhaps more, I heard my colleagues from Quebec mention the difficulties which our industries in Quebec and Canada are facing, and the best example I can give is that I heard the hon. member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) and the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier) say this afternoon that they regretted and deplored the decision taken by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) with respect to a particular industry in their regions. Well, I have one at home and it is the footwear industry.
Those members who sit on the government side have been down on their knees over the past few days and again this afternoon urging the minister to pay special attention to the footwear industry. That makes sense because it is now obvious that the measures announced by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce fall far short of the mark. Just as I did not so long ago during question period, they acknowledged that we have already lost 4,000 jobs in that sector since 1981 and that the corrective steps or measures announced by the minister just will not solve the problem. So now the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is being urged to reconsider those measures. I therefore hope that all hon. members, particularly our colleagues on the government side, will convince him that the situation has to be reviewed.
As can be seen in the industry and elsewhere, Mr. Speaker, the budget measures are not quite the remedy required in this case. This is where we have to make a choice when a measure
December 8, 1981

is introduced, and we can certainly not congratulate the Minister of Finance when we known full well that practically every day those small and medium-sized businesses have to shut down. Of course, the government will say that it has created thousands of jobs over the past five, ten or fifteen years. The fact remains that 15 years ago we had 300,000 idle workers in this country whereas we now have over one million. Something is amiss. During that period, the country was run almost entirely by the same party. I think the citizens of this country have a right to question the ability of this government and to deny it its confidence. Members on this side of the House obviously cannot put their confidence in a government which shows such blatant incompetence and which has failed once again to bring down a budget likely to restore confidence and reassure the Canadian people. I hope that when the budget bills are introduced in the House a majority of members will be able to bring the government back to reason and force it, by way of legislation, to improve the proposals made, which, in our opinion, are simply not good enough.
Finally, and I will end on this note, I cannot forget the confidence that the voters of Joliette recently put in me when I asked them to tell the government that it had failed with regard to interest rates, the fight against inflation and also with respect to energy costs, in particular the cost of gas. I will not go back to the constitutional vision, as we have just passed a resolution on that. Last August 17, Mr. Speaker, the riding of Joliette, through thousands of voters, asked me to give the government the message that the people were dissatisfied, that they could no longer tolerate the lack of adequate measures with regard to the present economic situation. It is clear, even though the government does not want to admit it to the people, that we are facing very hard months ahead. It is clear that the budget will not correct nor reverse the trend. It is also clear that unemployment will increase in the next few months. I may be accused of being pessimistic, but I think it is important for the people of Canada to realize that this government is incapable of the economic leadership required to remedy the situation.
Considering, as I say, that unemployment will increase and that the economic situation will only worsen, I can only hope that in the short term we will take the opportunity to show the government our disapproval of the blatant incompetence it has shown during the last decade. That is it. I will give others the opportunity to take part in this debate, but I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that on behalf of all my constituents and of thousands of Canadians, I do not intend to support this budget and pretend that we can have confidence in a government that has been deceiving us for so long with measures that are inadequate and incapable of improving the present situation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, budgets such as the one presented on November 12 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) are quite complicated documents and deserve thoughtful attention. This is particularly
The Budget-Mr. Blaikie
true of some of those aspects of the budget which are not easily understood and which are not readily identifiable as affecting the immediate self-interests of individuals or groups but which, nevertheless, have a great impact on the lives of all Canadians.
A good example of such an area of concern, to which there is devoted a separate document in the budget papers, is the area of federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, a subject I hope I will be able to reflect upon usefully in the next thirty minutes in the context of the proposals of the Liberal government. It is a concern which I hope will command some attention, as I look at an empty press gallery, even though it must compete with such highlights as inadequate mortgage legislation, the dogmatic monetarism of the Liberal Party, tax changes supposedy for the sake of equity which hurt the middle class but leave the rich unscathed, and the shameless retreat of the Liberal Party from the pursuit of controlling our own economy.
Nevertheless, the two aspects of federal-provincial fiscal arrangements which I wish to address today are established programs financing and the cuts which the government proposes in these transfer payments to the provinces and equalization payments, or the equalization formula, and the proposal of the Liberal government to use Ontario as the standard to which all other provinces will be equalized.
I feel much more qualified to comment on these matters than I would have prior to last spring, at which time I had the opportunity of being the New Democratic Member of Parliament on the seven-person, all-party special parliamentary task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangments which released the report entitled "Fiscal Federalism in Canada" on August 30. As a task force we visited all ten provincial capitals as well as the capitals in the territories, in addition to three weeks of public hearings here in Ottawa. It was a tremendous learning experience for me about Canada, about federalism and about what has been called the nuts and bolts of Canadian federalism, the fiscal arrangements which provide for the existence of many programs and services which Canadians take for granted.
However, at the end of a long and sometimes difficult process the task force produced a unanimous report, and later I hope I shall have cause to refer to some of the recommendations in our report.
The established programs financing, hereinafter in my speech referred to as EPF, is that part of federal-provincial fiscal arrangements which provides federal funding to the provinces in the form of block funding for those services which come under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, the Medical Care Act and federal support for postsecondary education.
In 1977 health and post-secondary education shared cost programs were integrated in a block-funding arrangement between the federal government and the provinces. The purpose of this significant change was twofold. It was to provide the federal government with more fiscal predictability than it had under previous arrangements wherein its spending was directly related to provincial spending, and in the same way

December 8, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Blaikie
the new arrangements were to act as a ceiling for the federal government, which was a form of restraint. I think it is important to note that the restraint began back in 1977, not in 1981.
There were also a number of benefits for the provincial governments in the new arrangement in 1977. They would not have to spend a dollar in order to get a dollar from the federal government, as they did under the shared cost programs, thus giving them more incentive to reduce costs. And with block funding they would be freer to innovate, unencumbered by the task of having to meet federal cost sharing criteria, a task which sometimes distorted provincial priorities. If they could receive cost sharing for the provision of acute care beds and not for chronic care beds, they tended to provide more acute care beds and neglect the need for chronic care beds. That is just an example of what I mean by distorting provincial priorities.
The block funding arrangement for health care and postsecondary education has received much criticism since 1977. Basically these criticisms have focused on the fact that the percentage of provincial spending on health care and postsecondary education has gone down significantly since 1977, with a corresponding decrease in the quality and availability of these services. Unfortunately, most provinces did not seize the opportunity to be creative in the new arrangement. Instead, they used their newfound spending autonomy to save money at the expense of the programs by allowing the guaranteed federal moneys to form a larger and larger percentage of spending in these areas. To a certain extent this is what they were supposed to do, according to the self-understanding of the 1977 EPF arrangements or agreements.
Again, unfortunately, most provinces went overboard, combining their new fiscal autonomy with the ideological zeal we witnessed in the late seventies on the part, mostly, of Progressive Conservative provincial governments, for cutbacks in government spending as the panacea for all our problems. It is, of course, a delusion which is still alive and well and seems recently to have been adopted by the Liberal government; but the point I wish to make is that EPF block funding never really had an opportunity to show its potential strength because its first five years coincided with this other historical and political phenomena. At this point we do not know, and cannot know as yet, whether the block funding could succeed in having the creative as well as the limiting effects it was supposed to have.
In any case, over the last few years there have been great arguments between federal and provincial governments about their respective contributions to health care and post-secondary education. The federal government has made much of its increasing percentage spending in this area and expressed increasing concern about cutbacks in health care and policies which seemed to retreat from, rather than advance toward, the perfection of medicare as a universal health care program available to rich and poor alike. Provinces argued, on the other hand, that the federal government was being self-righteous, that the provinces were only doing what they were expected to do under the 1977 agreement and that, furthermore, the EPF money was not as earmarked as the federal government
claimed it was. For instance, the provinces argued that the federal division of the EPF program money into two thirds for health care and one third for post-secondary education was arbitrary. Furthermore, in 1977 there was money in the EPF package which had been included in the package as compensation for the termination of an old agreement called the revenue guarantee. The money attributable to the revenue guarantee was particularly unconditional, argued the provinces. It was unfair, they claimed, for the federal government to use this money in the calculation of its spending on health care and post-secondary education relative to the provinces' contributions.
The provinces should have known that they might come to regret this line of argument, as I am sure they now do. The federal government has now adopted their arguments and the provinces are left to ponder the wisdom of their former pronouncements.
In his proposals for fiscal arrangements in the 1980s, the Minister of Finance proposes to cut federal transfer payments to the provinces by an amount equal to that attributable to the revenue guarantee in the EPF block fund, a reduction of some $5.7 billion over five years. The Minister of Finance argues two things in this respect. He argues that, after all, the revenue guarantee was not earmarked for health care and post-secondary education; thus adopting a version of things, in my view, which goes against the theory and against the statistics this government has been using for five years. The Minister of Finance also argues, knowing the frailty of his first argument and feeling guilty about it, that a good portion of this loss to the provinces will be made up by increased revenues to the provinces as a result of tax changes in the budget, leaving the provinces with only about a $2 billion loss over five years, provided that the government's economic forecast, not known for their accuracy, are actually accurate and not overly optimistic. Even according to the figures used by the Minister of Finance, a province such as my own province, Manitoba, would come out $75 million short at the end of the next five year fiscal arrangement. This is not an insignificant amount of money when one considers a have not province such as Manitoba.
The debate over fiscal arrangements is not a matter of siding with either the federal government or the provinces. This is something that I, as a member of the opposition, feel one should not get into. It is just not that simple, as I have tried to show. There are aspects of the fiscal arrangements that I do not even have the time to go into this afternoon. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that both sides have been less than honest in the way they have presented the problem to the public.
The only side that I feel obliged to come down on is the side of the programs themselves and the people of Canada who look to health care and post-secondary education as established programs for the healing and for the teaching of Canadians that no inter-governmental dispute should be able to threaten.
December 8, 1981

In this respect, I now call on the federal government to recall its proposed cutbacks for three reasons. The first reason is that there is no need for them in the first place. The federal government is anticipating new revenues as a result of the energy agreement, and besides, these programs have not been the cause of the deficit. They have not grown out of proportion to government spending as a whole. These programs cannot be blamed for the deficit. The federal government could also, if it wanted to make up the amounts of money that it proposes to save through the cancellation of the revenue guarantee, raise new moneys through the closing of corporate tax loopholes, the ones they left unclosed in this budget while slamming middle-income working people. And the federal percentage of spending in health care and post-secondary education will decrease even if the present arrangements were to continue, because the federal contribution is tied to the economy, while the provincial contribution is tied to inflation. Even if things were to continue as they are now, the federal contribution to these programs would decrease further. The Minister of Finance should be well satisfied if he could convince the provinces to continue the existing arrangements.
The second reason that I appeal to the Minister of Finance to recall his cutbacks is that if he is serious about having the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) negotiate the clarification and enforcement of national standards for medicare, such as the banning of extra billing by physicians, the discontinuance of user fees and. even the abolition of premiums, the Minister of Finance must not then be trying to take money off the table at the same time as the Minister of National Health and Welfare is trying to put more expensive standards on the table.
The third reason that I call on the minister to recall the proposed cutbacks is that there will be some provinces that will, quite beyond whatever legitimate anger they may express at the federal proposals, use the cutbacks to justify further cutbacks in their own commitment to these programs, while blaming the federal government.
Like it or not, Mr. Speaker, there are Progressive Conservative provincial governments in this country that still resent the existence of medicare. I say this with regret. I am not making a partisan speech when I say this. This is a political and philosophical fact, and the governments of Alberta, Ontario, and others of the same ilk should not, in the name of comprehensive federal restraint, be carelessly adding fuel to the fires they would like to set under Canada's medicare system. That is what the Minister of Finance is now doing with these cutbacks. These Progressive Conservative governments, along with the paranoid, red-necked, intellectually impoverished leadership of the Canadian Medical Association, who do great disservice to all the doctors I have ever known, pose the greatest danger to medicare. Together they represent that group of people who have not been able to put their ideological hobby horses aside and accept the will of the Canadian people that there be a publicly-funded health care system in Canada second to none in the world.
The Budget-Mr. Blaikie
I call on the provinces not to compound the stress they have already placed on these programs by cutting back even more than they have already. The federal response to provincial restraint, it seems, has been cutbacks of their own. To that I say that two wrongs do not make a right. If the provincial response to these cutbacks is more cutbacks, then I can only say that three wrongs do not make a right.
Earlier I referred to the Government of Ontario as being, among others, dangerous to the future wellbeing of medicare, and to Ontario, for that matter. If there was ever any doubt about this, it was completely erased last week when the health minister of that province announced new hospital policies that would have the effect of making fewer beds available to Canadians without private health insurance. The privatization of health care in Ontario is well under way. The Frank Millers and Dennis Timbrells can hardly contain their obscene delight that this is finally going on. They did not like medicare in the first place. They did not have the guts to levy the corporate taxes that would have paid for medicare, even when they grudgingly accepted it, and now they are perversely pleased when economic perceptions, to which the Minister of Finance is carelessly contributing with his cutbacks, give them the pretext for further dismantling of publicly funded health care in Ontario where medicare has always had only a tenuous foothold.
Ontario is one of the three provinces-and I probably do not have to remind members-and the others are Alberta and B.C., where medicare premiums are still paid, a form of paying for medicare which the all-party task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements found to be regressive and regrettable.
The state of medicare in Ontario brings me to the second topic with which I should like to deal today-the proposals of the Minister of Finance concerning equalization.
The new equalization plan whereby Ontario will become the standard to which have-not provinces are equalized is a very dangerous proposal in my view. Economically, if it is true that Ontario is becoming a have-not province, then other have-not provinces are tied to a sinking ship. From another standpoint, using Ontario's taxation and public services policies as a national model is dangerous indeed. Ontario's taxation and social policies are not value neutral but represent the accumulated values and decisions of decades of Conservative government. To suggest that this is the national average or the national model is an affront to all those who seek improvements and shows ignorance of the extent to which all such policies are formed by philosophical choices. For instance, as I have already indicated, Ontario drastically undertaxes its resource sector and wants to privatize health care. Is this the standard to which all provinces should be equalized? I think not. In fact, I find the whole idea repulsive in the extreme for reasons of both practice and principle, as I have said. Besides, this proposal of the government vis-a-vis making Ontario the model for equalization goes against the recommendation of the

December8, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Blaikie
Task Force on Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements that the new equalization formula not discriminate against any one province. The proposed formula discriminates against Ontario by definition and is therefore theoretically suspect on the basis of this recommendation alone. A new equalization formula will no doubt have to be found. I am well aware of the problems which exist with the old one. It will not be easy, but equalization is an important aspect of Canadian history, of Canadian federalism and of our new Constitution. Equalization payments to the provinces are entrenched in the new Constitution, but making the entrenched conservatism of Ontario the standard to which, hopefully, more enlightened parts of the country must conform would indeed be a mistake.
In this respect I should like to respond to the remarks made in the House by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) who was chairman of the special task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. In his speech on November 13 he stated:
In fact, it can be said that basically the federal proposals are in line with our recommendations.
I think this statement by the hon. member for Gloucester, the chairman of the task force on which I sat, is highly debatable. The hon. member was a good chairman. He helped produce a report which recommended against any cutbacks in federal support to health care and post-secondary education. It was a report which I believe went far in stopping the more draconian measures brewing on the back burner of the mysterious mind of the Minister of Finance. The hon. member for Gloucester shoud not now blur the glimpse we have had of him as an independent spirit by pretending that the government followed the recommendations of the task force. The task force indicated:
By virtue of the federal government's own internal allocation, all fiscal transfers associated with the revenue guarantee must now be considered part of the health care and post-secondary education package, and should therefore be allocated, in the renewed EPF arrangements, to health and/or post-secondary education in proportions to be negotiated.
How does the hon. member for Gloucester square that recommendation with the fact that the budget says the revenue guarantee was never allocated the way the task force obviously said it was, and that, furthermore, this budget proposes cutbacks against which the task force recommended and proposes to cut money the task force indicated must be seen to be part of the health care and post-secondary education package? People who have read the report entitled "Fiscal Federalism in Canada" and people who have read the budget document presented by the Minister of Finance entitled "Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements in the 80s" will not be tricked by the facile optimism of the hon. member for Gloucester.
Although I have dealt primarily with fiscal arrangements, I should like to wind up by calling on the Minister of Finance to respond in a general way to the almost unanimous condemnation of his budget by Canadians, whether they be home owners, tenants, workers, small businessmen or farmers. I want him to respond to the unanimous condemnation of the budget and to announce soon some significant changes in the budget which will be sensitive to the condemnation the budget
has received. He has indicated that he might consider some actions. Every once in a while we get a glimpse of reflection that perhaps he is actually thinking something over. I want to second the call of my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), for an immediate excess profits tax on the banks, a measure which could raise some $700 million right away, making money available for housing, interest rate relief, job creation and many of the things left undone in the budget as it stands now. An excess profits tax on banks would still leave banks at the profit rate level they had last year, which was already too high and would make the average corporation green with envy.
I support the criticisms of all those who have pointed to the way in which the budget, rather than being fair and equitable, is actually an attack on the hard-earned savings and retirement plans of many average Canadians. The loopholes closed by the government have been selective indeed, but the government selected the wrong people in most instances.
The budget deserves all the criticism it gets. I look forward, along with other members of the New Democratic Party caucus, to Committee of the Whole House wherein we will get a chance to tear it to shreds.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to add a few comments to those of my colleagues about the budget which was presented on November 12 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). This afternoon, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) asked if anyone could reassure Canadians with respect to this budget. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that I am better qualified than he, at any rate, to do so. The fact is that when the hon. member for Joliette was sitting on the government side, the then Minister of Finance had tabled such a budget that they were voted out.
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that that budget had a disastrous impact on the hon. member for Joliette, because at that time, such regressive measures as an 18-cent tax on gasoline brought the downfall of the previous government, and why was that, Mr. Speaker? They have been talking for a few days now about the bad housing situation in Canada. They conveniently forget that when they were in power, they had proposed doing away with no less than the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, Mr. Speaker, a basic agency which is responsible for monitoring the housing situation in Canada. Right now, our economic growth is not as rapid as in the early seventies, and most economists agree on that point, but it is a long way from justifying the hon. member's pessimism ... Not only has the Liberal government relied on the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, but the present budget has included a program which will bring 15,000 more units and a subsidy of $7,500 per rental unit with an interest-free loan, and, according to existing programs, 25,000 units, already provided for by the CMHC, within the co-operative housing and non profit rental accommodation programs, will be made
December 8, 1981

available. So, we can see, Mr. Speaker, that 40,000 housing units will be ready for occupancy. I think those policies will meet the needs of the Quebec people and that the building industry in that province will avail itself of those measures.
Single family home owners, as far as the Montreal-Mercier riding is concerned, are in some cases experiencing difficulties and I hope the program put forward by the minister concerned, will be of assistance to them. Any home owner who has to invest more than 30 per cent of his income on housing, will qualify for a special interest rate on his mortgage. Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, most of the people in my constituency are not home owners and as their representative I shall oppose a universal financing program for mortgage loans which would bring down the present interest rate of approximately 18 per cent down to 13.14 or 12 per cent, as it used to be, because in so doing we would have to take one billion dollars or more out of the taxpayers' pockets. I think that no responsible government can present a balanced, non inflationary budget and at the same time include additional taxes to pay for the mortgages of home owners. However, I am well aware of the problems and I urge the people of my constituency to contact the department. A special service has been set up to help them if the burden of the debt were to become overpowering. Among the positive aspects of this budget, let us mention the $210 tax reduction that on the average 12,000,000 taxpayers will be granted. It is almost wizardry, nowadays, to get a budget which cuts on taxes. Yet not only does the budget allow tax cuts but more than 3.2 billion dollars will find their way back into the taxpayers' pockets through income tax indexing. This means Canadians will not be penalized by inflation since taxation will be adjusted as it was in the past. Evidently our opposition friends a few weeks before the budget was tabled, raised the spectre of the elimination of indexation and today forget to mention the important fact that Canadian taxpayers will not have to pay those additional 3.2 billion dollars.
And for the Quebec people, Mr. Speaker, it is even more important, because for years the so-called soicialist, or social democratic government of Quebec has been talking about full indexation of income tax rolls but has never implemented it. On the other hand, this Liberal government that I am proud to work with, keeps maintaining this indexation which means so much to the workers of the Montreal-Mercier constituency.
Other major programs have been not only retained but indexed, Mr. Speaker. For example, mothers in my riding can still benefit from the child endowment which is indexed on a three-month basis. A tax credit for their children will go up from $261 per child to $293 per child. Old age security pensions, which were increased in the last budget by $35 besides indexation, will continue to be indexed.
And another good piece of news for the Quebec workers: Each worker's contribution to the unemployment insurance will decrease from $1.80 to $1.65 while the employer's contribution will be reduced to $2.31.
The Budget-Mrs. Hervieux-Payette
Mr. Speaker, this budget reflects the Liberal philosophy, maintaining as it does the socially oriented programs which account for a large share of the federal budgetary envelope, and yet they will enable each family in Quebec to maintain a style and quality of life which all of us ought to be proud of. 1 suggest as well that the low-income families will be glad to learn that the $200 family deduction will be raised to $400-a 100 per cent increase. That increase is on top of all the other advantages that the average taxpayer in the province of Quebec will gain from this budget. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, a lot has been said in Quebec about fiscal arrangements. The finance minister has been very loquacious on that subject, somewhat less about his own taxes and slightly more about the contributions of that same federal government whose existence he denies. However, he forgets to mention that under the fiscal arrangements, over the next five years Quebec will benefit from an average annual increase of about 12.9 per cent. And then they often forget-and that makes me laugh a little, Mr. Speaker-that the so-called progressive university circles dismiss rather easily the contribution made by the federal government to their own budgets. Indeed, at the present time roughly 58 per cent of the funds budgeted by Quebec universities come from the federal government.
While, Mr. Speaker, there is reason to rejoice in the federal government's contributions to these programs, we must also ask ourselves how these programs are being administered by our province. In fact, Mr. Speaker, what is Quebec's record in this respect? As far as health insurance is concerned, any profits or benefits as a result of good administration of the program are transferred to the public treasury without benefit to the program itself, and as far as hospital insurance is concerned, although the federal government contributes to the program, under the Constitution hospital administration is a provincial responsibility, and the provincial government is not a good administrator. It has been making budget cuts every year and reducing the quality and especially the volume of care provided in Quebec. Where does Canada stand, Mr. Speaker, as far as per capita income is concerned compared with the rest of the world? A report by the Tribune magazine in one of the-

December 8, 1981
The Budget-Mrs. Hervieux-Payette [Translation]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose, I was about to quote figures from the 1981 World Almanac to show how Canadians rank on per capita income. According to my tables, Canada is fourth in the world out of 150 countries and Canadians have an average per capita income of $7,572. West Germany, the United States and France come, respectively, first, second and third.
Mr. Speaker, I think we can be proud of these statistics. However, in its November 14, 1981 issue, The Economist says that one of the problems facing Canada today and which this budget has had to face as well is inflation. I think that my constituents realize that massive budgetary spending might have increased inflationary pressures. Our colleagues opposite, of course, advocate sound conservative principles when they speak outside the House, but here they call for further spending, forgetting that the inflation rate during the last quarter has reached 12.5 per cent. But what does a 12.5 per cent inflation rate means when in the United States the rate is 11 per cent, in the Federal Republic of Germany, 7 per cent, and in the Netherlands, 6 per cent? I think that it means that the purchasing value of the dollar is eroded.
1 think that the budget shows that the Minister of Finance is realistic and responsible when he wants to extend social measures while attempting to reduce our deficit over a five-year period. I must not forget to mention the value of our currency, because all those factors must be taken into consideration when a budget is being prepared. For example, let us consider what happened in the European Economic Community or in Europe when the German mark was recently devalued by 20 per cent, the French franc by 30 per cent, while last week the Canadian dollar was worth about 85 cents. I also feel that most Canadians agree to maintain that slight margin in relation to the American dollar.
I should like to point out to the hon. members that in terms of dollars, every dollar spent because of the monetary policy of the Minister of Finance will enable us to control inflation and to ensure finally that the weekly income of the constituents of Mercier, especially the aged, the single parent families, largely made up of women and children, is not affected. 1 feel that at present, the priority of the government is to provide every citizen with the required income to enjoy a minimum quality of life, to set fair and equitable tax rates, as does the budget and manage at the same time to reduce inflation in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, one of the major components of the budget is, of course, the national energy policy implemented by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) as well as the agreement entered into with Alberta. Since 1979, Canada was really not in a position to prepare a budget without that major component. I am pleased to note today that the Canadian government has signed that agreement with Alberta, even though the negotiations were difficult, even
though the previous government had never succeeded in reaching an agreement.
For the information of my constituents, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should mention some of the loopholes this budget intends to plug, to indicate what the Minister of Finance exactly had in mind when he set forth to abolish some of the exemptions that were granted to certain individuals. For instance, Quebec taxpayers are already contributing to a dental insurance plan for children aged from 0 to 16. This coverage is already provided, and some $50 millions have already been paid by Quebec taxpayers. Also, a number of employers, through collective agreements, are providing their employees with free dental care programs. These are benefits which are not included in the income and which will be taxable from now on. Mr. Speaker, as a Canadian living in Quebec I think I am already paying taxes to provide my children with dental care, and that it is only fair that if such benefits are to be provided to some people, they should not be provided to only one class of citizens, as it is the case now, a very small group of workers who benefit from collective agreements, as only 30 per cent of workers are now unionized and are entitled as such to free dental programs.
Here is another example, Mr. Speaker, of benefits which will be taxable from now, I mean, in the case of a taxpayer who owns two houses. Previously, a well-advised citizen could quite legally buy a first house and register it under his own name, then buy himself a house in the country and register it in his wife's name. I think that this was the way it went most of the time, although in some cases, there are wives who have bought second houses and registered them in the names of their husbands. So when he or she sold both houses, there were no taxable gains because the houses had been registered under two different names. From now on, it is the family unit that will be taken into account under the new taxation system. The capital gains, therefore, on the second house will become taxable. I think that the taxpayers in my riding of Mercier will feel that this is quite fair, for I do not see how they could support a second residence for other Canadians or would provide them with special benefits, when some of them cannot even afford good quality housing. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I am also aware that some business executives were receiving interest-free loans. I too would have liked to see my constituents in Montreal-Mercier go to the bank and borrow $100,000 without paying interest. The old provisions in our fiscal law allowed corporations to lend tremendous amounts, as high as $100,000, without tax being levied on that interest benefit. I feel that this budget is simply reintroducing equity for Canadians. The 12 million taxpayers who were granted a tax reduction through this budget cannot but agree. As far as I am concerned, I must state that in my constituency I received only one letter, and it came not from a firm but from a business association. I can understand that some adjustments have to be made. I can understand that some non-discrimina-

tory interpretations have to be drawn, and I believe the initiatives in the new budget will be interpreted in a fair and equitable way by the Minister of Finance.
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) raised the matter of the urea-formaldehyde foam insulation, and he suggested the government should commit funds in that respect in the budget. I must state that as far as I am concerned, I have followed the situation very closely because in my constituency, I know of a number of victims. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) is now considering different measures to help those involved.
But what I would like to condemn at this point is the behavior of the hon. member for Joliette who in his capacity as the former Minister for Supply and Services, had agreed to an established standard for the use of that foam insulation under the previous government. And now, the hon. member has stood in his place and told us this afternoon that remedial actions had to be taken. I would point out that the product was allowed to be used when he was minister, and the people in the constituency of Joliette must know that the hon. member for Joliette approved that product. And if problems arose because of what may have been faulty application or installation, I feel that this government will take its responsibilities as it did with the budget. But I also think that this responsible government is not willing to commit $1 billion of the taxpayers' money to solve a problem where a much smaller amount may be needed.
Mr. Speaker, 1 have listened with great interest to the many well-documented comments made by my colleagues from the NDP on medicare programs. I must say how I sympathize but I find it passing strange that their arguments should always center on provincial programs and that they put so much emphasis on bank profits. I am not here to speak in defence of the banks, Mr. Speaker, and I do think that we passed an excellent piece of legislation on that matter earlier in this session. I will leave it up to the Minister of Finance to decide whether he wants to consider this issue. Still I think that it is not with our hearts but with our heads that we must analyse this budget, and that is why I ask every member of this House to think that each and every citizen of his riding, each and every taxpayer, everyone in fact must have his or her fair share of the gross national product and of the wealth of this country, and that is why, Mr. Speaker, as a Quebecer I am proud to vote in favour of a budget such as this one.
