subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to add the concerns of the people of Waterloo riding to the national tide of dissatisfaction which has risen to greet this antisocial and regressive budget.
In a document which gives the government such an important opportunity to send out so many signals of its social policy, even those in my area who have supported the government so loyally for so long have found that there is nothing but a cold shoulder for the growing number of unemployed, the small family farmer, the low-income insurance policyholders, the small business community, and perhaps foremost is the sector of Canadian society made up of victims of this government's last budget and its continuing high interest rate policies. I refer, of course, to home owners. I refer also to those on fixed incomes, whether veterans, widows, single parent families or the elderly.
In this budget, which has been presented with such fine rhetoric, Canadians are blamed for inflation. They are force-fed with price increases. They are ignored if they are not working. They are taxed more if they are working. And they are forgotten if they are unable to work.
The most devastating of the finance minister's error in judgment is the one of omission. Nowhere in all the volumes that go to support this budget is there even the slightest bit of evidence that the minister, or his officials, who seem to have taken hold of him in the process, have ever considered giving encouragement to the voluntary sector.
On top of forcing cuts to community based centres and transition homes for women, the government refuses to maintain and to widen caring alternatives, which are supplied across our nation by the voluntary community. Already faced with staggering increases in the operating overhead as a result of the government's refusal to offset unprecedented postal rate increases, the voluntary sector-the YMCAs, the Cancer Society, the Red Cross and the churches-is being overloaded and discouraged just when the need is greatest for their goods and services.
It is not surprising that in recent days those looking at the fabric of our Canadian society see the potential for a great deal of social violence and social strife. Already instances of family violence are up as family after family seeks to make ends meet just to provide the basics.
At a time when unemployment in Kitchener-Waterloo, in the surrounding area and generally in southwestern Ontario, has never been greater, this budget does not create even one job. As my colleague, the hon. member for Cambridge (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
December 8, 1981
The Budget-Mr. McLean
Speyer) said on November 18, "There is no reason to believe that this government wants Canadians to believe they have the right to make a living".
My colleague, the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), former minister of agriculture, pointed out on November 19 that the Minister of Finance's (Mr. MacEachen) elimination of the income-averaging annuity contracts and the capital gains tax reserve has tragically penalized the retirement income of the Canadian farmer.
It would seem clear that no one in this government understands the fact that a farmer's retirement income lies in the sale of his land. No other segment of Canadian society has its retirement income so severely taxed. According to the government's own Statistics Canada figures, Canadian farmers will bear the brunt of the economic effects. Their net income is expected to drop by about 15 per cent. Farm operating costs will rise faster than the return on the sale of farm products. On top of this must be added the hidden costs of energy price increases, which alone will account for a 2 per cent increase in food prices. These have not been offset by any form of energy tax credit, a feature in the Crosbie budget. The Crosbie budget now looks much more humane and compassionate in terms of the human and social side of its proposals, which brings me to this government's assault on the ability of low-income Canadians to plan a family's financial security.
At the national pensions conference held in Ottawa in April, the Minister of Finance had some interesting comments. Fie said:
I think it is universally agreed that private pension plans will continue to play a vital role in the retirement income system.
The effect of inflation on private pension plans is perhaps one of the most difficult problems that we face. I think we must deal with the harmful effect inflation can have on those with pensions from employer-sponsored pension plans and on those people in our society who are least able to protect themselves from inflation.
Finally he said:
The federal government, acting alone, cannot give Canada a retirement system geared to suit the expectations and the needs of Canadians.
Despite those statements, Mr. Speaker, made just over six months ago, the Minister of Finance, acting alone, has, without warning, knocked the bottom out of the private pension market, employer-sponsored pension schemes and the retirement plans of millions of Canadians. To rearrange the minister's own words, the federal government, acting alone, can give Canada a retirement system completely unsuited to the needs and expectations of Canadians.
Another of the many areas with which this budget has tinkered so callously is that of support for health care and post-secondary education. The budget includes an attempt to reduce the federal government's obligation to assist in the financing of health and post-secondary education by $5.7 billion over the next five years. We all remember now that on budget night the Minister of Finance argued that such reductions would be offset by $3,790 billion in additional tax revenues to be collected by provincial governments. Already he
has revised this figure downward by $662 million, meaning that provincial tax revenues will be raised by $3,128 billion, but they will have $2,562 billion less to use in the health care system and for the Canadian community colleges and universities.
It is indeed ironic that after justifying the new energy taxes, which are part of the agreements they signed with the governments of Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan, on the grounds that the national government had to be able to distribute energy wealth across the country more equitably, this budget does not propose to spend one cent of the $7.5 billion additional revenue on either health care or post-secondary education. Indeed, the budget proposes to save government money at the expense of these two social programs.
I am urging, within my own riding of Waterloo, the University of Waterloo, Wilfrid Laurier University and Conestoga College, just as I urge the representative bodies from the sector of post-secondary education across the nation, not to be deluded by the finance minister's subtle and confusing schemes. Just as this budget includes no job creation incentives, neither do our community colleges receive extra funding for retraining initiatives and programs geared to the thousands of Canadian women who are seeking to re-enter the work force.
I should like to say that the mail I have received from Kitchener, from Waterloo and from the townships of Woolwich, Wellesley and Wilmot which I represent, and from across Canada since this insensitive budget was introduced, is overwhelming. It outlines the unnecessary suffering the budget inflicts on those in our society who are least able to cope. Here, is just one of several examples: I quote from a letter written to the Hon. Paul Cosgrove, minister for housing. It states in part:
There are few words strong enough to express my displeasure with both the current state of economic affairs and the recent budget. You see, I am one of the unfortunate individuals whose mortgage renewed at high interest rates. To be precise, on August 25, 1981 at 21'/2 per cent, up from 93/4 per cent. On a mortgage of approximately $44,000, the interest rate increase meant monthly payments would increase by approximately $400 in after tax dollars.
Further on the letter goes on to read:
The disappointment you have created in hundreds of individuals who put their trust in you is beyond comprehension ... it's criminal and I am both angry and depressed. Here are some alternatives:
(B) Sell and rent. Almost a (zero) per cent vacancy rate in this area.
(E) Sell more annuities and life insurance, my profession, to earn additional income. Although I'm working night and day to reach that objective, I guess it goes without saying that Mr. MacEachen's budget has blocked this alternative, the repercussions of which will be monumental and will become apparent in the immediate future.
I have another letter which has come to me from the head office of a National Company, Home Hardware. The general manager of that collection of entrepreneurial and energetic hardware operators across the country writes in this letter, addressed to Mr. MacEachen:
The provisions in your recent budget to transfer the collection of the Federal Sales Tax to the wholesaler is one that perplexes our industry-
December 8, 1981

Transferring the tax to the wholesale industry will increase the paper-work burden by more than 1,000 fold ... We urge you to reconsider this very costly proposal until it can be studied more fully by government and the industry . .. the tax should be applied on the acquisition cost and not on the wholesale selling price.
Again, Mr. Speaker, from across this area of Canada, full of representatives of working people in our industries, representatives of small business people, comes another letter which states in part:
Why are you removing the incentive for the small business?
This person goes on, as he sees the dilution of his Canadian dream, in these terms:
The shame of it all is that we are a consulting firm specializing in productivity improvement, something this country and your government needs badly. We are very successful in this and are having good results in the immediate area which, as you know, suffers from severe economic problems, plant shut downs, lay-offs, etc. However, your budget is destroying us and the people we are trying to serve. You may have been out to catch the super rich, but you caught us in the same net.
The budget, in its efforts to come to terms with the importance of responsibility in government planning, has done something which the previous budget presented by those on this side sought, has not balanced restraint with compassion. It has not offsets for those who are hurt the most.
Since the finance minister is so interested in bottom lines, as he is fond of saying, and not in social costs, let me conclude by giving him a message relating to both on behalf of the people of Waterloo riding whom I represent. This budget offers no incentive for people to invest either for themselves or of themselves. I urge the minister to withdraw the budget and realize the disastrous social effects it is having upon the morale of the people of this nation.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the over-all intent of my remarks tonight will be to point out some of the very tangible benefits of this budget for the native people. But first, as far as the general thrust of the remarks by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in his budget speech is concerned, it is of no less interest to the native and northern Canadians than to others. It seems to me that the task of crafting a national economic policy requires the meshing together of a multitude of considerations into a coherent over-all policy. I congratulate my colleague for his general approach to the economy and I also thank him for the consideration which his budget showed for the particular interests of those Canadians whom I represent in cabinet.
As the Minister of Finance said, the budget has three main themes: equity, restraint and economic renewal. The budget embodies two measures which will have a direct impact on natives and northerners in which these themes are clearly evident. These three elements of the budget package are combined in its approach to native economic development. According to the government's fiscal plan until 1985-86, a sum of $345 million has been reallocated from the Western Development Fund to the social affairs envelope to meet the needs of the economic objectives of the native people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How much was that?
The Budget-Mr. J. Munro

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is $345 million. Indian people have demonstrated a growing capacity to capitalize on economic development opportunities over the past decade. Wherever I go these days, I hear native leaders describe economic development as a remedy for their peoples' social ills. Perhaps jobs and money in peoples' pockets is not the only answer, but I am satisfied that the systematic identification and exploitation of economic opportunity is one of the single most promising approaches available to us. I am indeed pleased that by agreeing to reassign moneys on the scale which was mentioned in the budget, my colleagues have made a major resource commitment in this direction.
Over the past few years, native leaders have substantially contributed to the evolution of a national approach to break the old cycle of welfare dependence. Together, we have been able to identify significant economic and employment opportunities. Our research indicates an on-reserve potential for thousands of jobs for Indians if we can build on the resources of reserves. The off-reserve potential for native people to be gainfully employed is estimated to be similar, according to our findings.
Through experience, some of it admittedly bitter, we have been able to isolate several limitations to past economic development strategies which were designed for the Indian people. Our primary conclusion was that they have not always had enough control over their own social and economic development and have not had the chance to shape it to their own particular values and widely varying needs. We must ensure that this does not happen again.
Another major impediment to encouraging appropriate economic development has been the absence of one essential ingredient, which is money. All the potential that Indian people can muster will not create jobs and wealth to get them on the road to recovery of their self-reliance without the money to make it happen. In the past, the funds necessary to generate native-run ventures have too often been consumed by the relentless demands of the welfare cycle. The government is taking a positive step in the right direction by setting aside the money identified in this budget. This is the proper direction to follow because Indian people have played a substantial part in its choice. In short, the government has shown the political will to direct a major portion of its new financial allocations toward economic development for native peoples.
To return to the main themes of the budget and how it benefits another group of people for whom I am responsible in cabinet, it is evident also that the principle of equity in taxation has particular significance to northern Canadians. I feel it is vital for northerners to understand that principle which is at stake in taxation of northern benefits. I want to do what I can in the House to clarify this issue and help people make sense of what some may fear is simply just a withdrawal of federal support to people living and working in the north, so I hope that hon. members will bear with me for a moment.
Above all, I want to assure the House that every effort will be made to see that the special needs of northerners are

December 8, 1981
The Budget-Mr. J. Munro
answered in a way that is compatible with Canada's tax system.
I recall with some vividness my first tour of the north as Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in the early 1980s. I remember clearly the anxiety and sincerity with which I was greeted in numerous communities during that tour which coincidentally closely followed an administrative decision to eliminate the customary exemption of northern benefits which had been permitted until then. I, for one, Mr. Speaker, remain convinced of the necessity for finding an equitable solution.
As you know by now, a decision has been taken to discontinue the temporary remission from taxation of certain employee benefits accorded to people working in the north and in isolated posts. That remission order, or moratorium, was due to expire on December 31, 1981. After that date, low-cost housing benefits, subsidized housing allowances and travel assistance in respect of transportation and medical purposes would have become taxable like any other income.
The effect of the budget, then, is, first, to extend the moratorium for another year until December 31, 1982. The tax relief is limited to those benefits that are granted under employer-employee agreements reached before this budget was announced. All such benefits will become taxable as income from employment effective January 1, 1983. The extension will allow sufficient time for employers and employees who are directly affected by this decision to negotiate the required adjustment.
Second, beginning with the 1982 taxation year, and for the following years, the list of qualifying deductible medical expenses will be extended to include travel costs incurred by residents in isolated areas so that they may receive medical services which are not available to them in their region. I welcome this measure which contributes toward improving the fairness in the accessibility in the medical services for all Canadians wherever they may live.
It is well known that in order to attract experienced workers in the north and other remote areas, industry and governments have to offer higher financial incentives. The present system favours employees represented by unions which negotiate nontaxable benefits which are added to their members' basic wages. For the majority of employees who are not represented by unions, the additional financial incentive offered to them by small employers to work in the north has been built into their basic wages and consequently has been fully taxed. This clearly is unfair and unacceptable.
The cost of living in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon affects all northerners to some degree. Therefore, any measure to assist them should benefit everyone, and, preferably, it should be related to their economic status.
As indicated in the budget, the delay of one year will allow the government to have adequate time to review the need for and the means of providing special assistance to employees working in the north and in isolated posts. I am pleased to say that I have been assigned this responsibility and that I have
already instructed my officials to look, in co-operation with officials of other departments, at possible means of responding to the special needs of northerners in a way that is compatible with Canada's tax system. The difficulty we are faced with is how to offset termination of the moratorium without creating a precedent in the national personal income tax policy. I am confident we will find a solution in the ensuing years.
I have followed closely the budget debate and the public comment over the last four weeks. I have been impressed by the one conclusion that must be reached by any hon. member who is prepared to deal with the economic facts. The undeniable truth is that nothing which has been said in the debate undermines the fundamental premise of the budget as presented by my colleague, the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance set out to establish-convincingly, I believe-that there can be no deep and lasting relief from our current economic ills, including high levels of unemployment, slow economic growth rates and high interest rates, until inflation is reduced. We must do all we can to bring down the rate of inflation. This is what the measures introduced by the budget will help bring about, if we give them a chance. As my colleague, the Minister of Finance, stated in the House:
We will generate less employment, less growth and more unemployment if we attempt to live with inflation than if we resolve once and for all to see it steadily reduced.
As a trading nation, Canada has no choice but to follow this policy with determination. All hon. members are aware, but it bears repeating, that Canada is an open economy; 25 per cent to 30 per cent of our gross national product is generated by exports. If we are to remain competitive with our major trading partners, we have to make sure that the rate of inflation in this country does not exceed that of our competition. This is particularly the case at this time. The principal policy objective of the United States, which accounts for about 70 per cent of our exports, is to break the back of inflation. This is what the United States government believes it must do in order to put its own house in order and enable it to meet tough competition in its domestic and world markets. The current projection is that the United States may be able to achieve an inflation rate of 7.5 per cent to 8 per cent in 1982. This compares with an inflation rate in Canada of 12.7 per cent. Unless we are determined to bring our rate down, a gap of more than 4 per cent in the inflation rate between Canada and the United States will impose a severe burden on our ability to compete in our most important markets.
As a Member of Parliament from a so-called steel city, 1 know this could a have a major impact of a deleterious kind in terms of steel production in that city and a more exaggerated and unfortunate impact on employment rates in the steel industry.
The budget reinforces the determination on the part of the government to take the lead in bringing down the rate of inflation. In the first place, the government is taking effective measures to reduce the budgetary deficit. We believe that the vast majority of Canadians support this endeavour, since too
December 8, 1981

great a share of tax revenue is now needed to service the national debt. This process was started in the October 1980 budget. It will move forward at an accelerated rate under the current fiscal plan. The deficit and financial requirements will be reduced by $2.9 billion, to a level of $10.5 billion in 1982-83, and there will be a further reduction in 1983-84.
By bringing down the deficit, the government will ease pressure on interest rates, the magnitude of this initiative and its potential for economical stimulation can be measured by the fact that the deficit amounts to 4 per cent of the gross national product this year and, according to the strategy under the current fiscal plan, this could be reduced to 1.9 per cent of the gross national product by 1985-86.
At the same time my colleague, the Minister of Finance, has made provision to continue to assist those Canadians who need government help and to ensure that the burden in the fight against inflation is shared equitably. This is done in a number of ways, first, it establishes a greater measures of equity in the taxes Canadians will pay starting next year. For example, by taking back some special privileges enjoyed by a minority of taxpayers it will make possible a reduction in taxes for about 12 million taxpayers. Taxes will be about the same for Vh million taxpayers, and they will be higher for fewer than
800,000.	The lower taxes for the majority of Canadians hopefully will provide new incentives for individuals to work, save and invest.
Second, the budget brings a significant measure of relief to Canadians who have been hard-pressed by high interest rates, including Canadians who are renewing their mortgages and small business proprietors and farmers who need to finance their operations. The government is allocating $400 million to help Canadians renewing their mortgages, to assist small businesses and farmers and to stimulate the construction of new rental units in metropolitan centres.
Third, the budget will continue the previous measures for indexing which have assisted taxpayers to meet increases in personal and family living costs due to inflation. For 1982, personal exemptions, tax brackets and the refundable child tax credit will rise by 12.2 per cent. The personal exemptions for a family of four will rise from $7,230 to $8,110 next year. The largest percentage benefit from indexing will go to lower-income taxpayers. The total benefit for all taxpayers will amount to more than $3 billion.
The budget must also be given credit for reinforcing a new economic climate that is responsible for bringing down interest rates. It does so, I believe, by giving the strong indication that our inflationary expections have been misguided. We can do something as a country to bring down the rate of inflation, and the reduction in interest rates which all Canadians want is bound to follow. We have already witnessed with a great sense of relief over the past few weeks and months a lowering of interest rates, which certainly is some indication of confidence in the direction we are taking with this economic policy.
As my colleague, the Minister of Finance, has indicated on a number of occasions, the budget measures will be examined in detail in Committee of the Whole. The government will be
The Budget-Miss Carney
guided by the three themes which were set out in the budget itself; namely, restraint in government spending, equity for all taxpayers and economic renewal. If all hon. members are motivated by the same considerations, I believe we will be in a good position to work toward the economic recovery this country badly needs and richly deserves.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to debate the very damaging and destructive budget which was tabled in this House on November 12 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). Events since then have shown that the budget has had a devastating impact on the economy of our country and on the lives of individual Canadians. The budget is so harmful that in the few short weeks since its introduction the Minister of Finance has been forced to acknowledge three major errors. He has had to change the rules affecting rental housing construction so that the 13,000 homes now under construction can proceed, he has had to give special dispensation to allow certain corporate takeovers to be completed under terms introduced in previous budgets, and he has had to confess to a $700 million error in the federal government's projections of lost provincial revenues. And that is only the start.
At a time of increasing unemployment, the minister has introduced measures which will severely cripple small business, which is one of the most important job-creating sectors of the economy. When nearly one million Canadians are out of work, he has threatened major industries such as the insurance industry, which employs thousands of Canadians, the construction industry and the forest industry. At a time of high interest rates he has brought in a budget which imposes new taxes on income before it is even received, forcing companies and individuals to go to the banks or bankruptcy courts. At a time when productivity is low he has introduced measures which create a tax structure which discriminates against young, expanding and innovative firms which need their cash reserves to finance their future growth and favours established, mature companies which have the resources to pay dividends. At a time when vast new sources of financing and saving are required to finance the projects we need to sustain our economy, he has wiped out incentives to investors. At a time when Canadianization is a goal of government, he has eliminated the right of Canadians to deduct interest on loans made to invest in Canadian companies and given foreign investors a clear advantage over Canadian investors. At a time when Canadians' confidence in the economy is at a 20-year low, the minister has launched a massive assault on our homes, our jobs and our savings. This is not merely my assessment of the havoc that he has created, Mr. Speaker, nor is it only the view of the major interest groups. It is the assessment of those Canadians who have to live with this budget.
Tonight I want you, Mr. Speaker, to hear some of the concerns that have been expressed. A good overview of the feeling of outrage in the country, was expressed by a voter in

December 8, 1981
The Budget-Miss Carney
the constituency of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He writes:
The Liberals are now proposing to tax the insurance policy income of widows and orphans, the deferred income savings of one-shot earners and the annuity build-ups of self-employed people who have no company pension fund or fat indexed civil service retirement scheme. This is a confiscation of property on a scale not seen since the days of the robber barons of the middle ages.
The general anxiety felt by many Canadians is expressed by the senior citizen who spent her life savings of $500 and borrowed more than $1,000 to buy a wheelchair.
She wrote me:
How on earth can I pay $1,000 back with the high cost of food, shelter and phone and now this dreadful budget? This budget is making everyone live in fear and fear is foreign to me.
One of the most fearful aspects of the budget is its impact on housing and construction. The budget has not done anything to relieve the critical shortage of housing in the country. Indeed, it has deliberately eliminated tax incentives which have encouraged the construction of rental housing in the 1970s.
The Rental Housing Council of B.C. notes that in the past when incentives were withdrawn, the bottom dropped out of housing development, and vacancy rates dropped to near zero. When the present tax incentives cease at the end of the year, housing experts predict a rental housing famine for years to come.
Tenants in Canada are already suffering from a shortage of accommodation and rising rents. There is the Vancouver apartment dweller whose rent has just increased 66 per cent, from $850 to $1390 per month, and who realizes that with the withdrawal of incentives for rental housing, he will be unable to find cheaper accommodation.
Then there is the case in my constituency of the three senior citizens whose rent is soaring by 70 per cent, from $235 per month to $400 per month, because their building has been sold and they are being forced to assume the burden of the refinancing costs.
There are agencies such as the Kitsilano housing registry in Vancouver, which is in my constituency, which is trying to find housing for single parents who are only able to pay $200 to $300 a month, in a market where a two-bedroom apartment rents from $600 to $900 a month and a one-bedroom apartment from $400 to $600.
The Greater Victoria Apartment Owners Association has advised the minister that without incentives rents on new units will double, and many tenants simply cannot afford to pay.
The association president, Robert Jawl, writes:
We think people who are forced to rent can be kept housed in decent shelter. Surely Canadians are not asking for favours when they ask that much.
When the then minister of finance, John Turner, introduced the capital cost allowance on MURBs in 1974, he said:
I am confident that this measure will attract a significant amount of private equity capital into the construction of new rental housing.
History has shown that Mr. Turner was correct. History will show that his successor, the present Minister of Finance, is
wrong in removing the incentives which have provided Canadians with homes in the past.
Another concern of individual Canadians is the elimination of the right to deduct interest on loans made to invest in Canadian companies. This right has existed since 1948. This right has been in place for 33 years. Its purpose for 33 years has been to provide an incentive to cautious Canadians to take a risk on the future of our country. This budget makes it a poor risk, since many Canadians have borrowed money and have made commitments in good faith based on measures that were introduced by the past Liberal governments. Now they find they face heavy tax penalties.
There is the college professor who has written the Minister of Finance in these terms:
Please help, 1 will be placed in a serious financial situation unless you reconsider a grandfather interest deductibility for commercial as well as residential investments.
He was a small investor with a few thousand dollars who borrowed to invest in a real estate partnership under the tax laws prevailing at the time. His anticipated interest costs for 1982 are $20,000, which represents a large share of his aftertax salary, his only source of income. The investment is not liquid and will not return any income until 1990. He writes:
It seems most unfair to change the law when I cannot alter my investment which was only feasible under the previous rules.
There were thousands of British Columbians who borrowed money from the chartered banks to take advantage of an opportunity to buy $400 million worth of shares in the British Columbia Resources Investment Corporation. That was the largest share issue in British Columbia's history. People bought their shares then at $6 each. The current market price is about $3.20, reflecting the depressed economy. Yet many small shareholders and first time investors find they can no longer deduct the interest on the money they borrowed to buy a share of their own provincial resources, unless they have other investment income.
Then there is the Canadian businessman who was trying to build a group of totally Canadian employee-owned businesses in Canada, who writes that the loss of interest deductibility will have a disastrous effect on his company's operations, growth and ability to maintain a Canadian presence against its foreign-owned competitors. He writes:
I, my 100 fellow shareholders and our 500 employees, many of whom aspire to future ownership and management in our companies, have never felt so betrayed or sabotaged in our efforts, as by our own government in the new proposed budget.
Buying a share in the company which employs them, thus helping them to secure their jobs, is the dream of many Canadians. That dream has been shattered by the elimination of interest deductibility for many Canadians.
There are all those Canadians who are writing the Minister of Finance for the first time to point out the unfairness of the government's move in changing rules after commitments have been made. One Canadian writes:

I am incensed that you have the gall to close the "rich man's loopholes", while only a few years ago, you referred to these loopholes, as "tax incentives for housing".
Previous Liberal ministers introduced these measures to encourage Canadians to invest in Canada, to provide for their own financial security and to help Canadians to own a greater share of their national resources and economy. History will show that these Liberal ministers have been right. History will show that the present Minister of Finance has been dead wrong.
The elimination of the interest deductibility is particularly destructive to the very sectors of the economy that this government has sought to encourage. Those companies which require all their cash resources to finance their expansion, and thus do not pay dividends, have been particularly savaged. This group includes junior oil and mining companies which require their funds for exploration and development and high technology companies which use their cash resources to develop new product lines and thus do not plan to pay dividends in their first few years of operation.
The president of one high-tech company, with offices in my constituency, wrote the minister:
The damage that will be done to the growth section of the Canadian economy, the largest provider of new jobs for Canadians, cannot be justified.
A Canadian who located and brought four mines into production in the last 25 years wrote the minister:
The move to propose to limit the deduction of an individual to the amount of his annual taxable investment income is absolutely insane.
Where do you think the majority of money comes from for the initial and secondary financing of the resource orientated companies of this resource rich country of Canada?
This budget removes the incentive to invest in our own country.
There are other measures in the budget which have dealt a bitter blow to many small businesses, many of whom must now pay tax on income before they actually receive it and whose sources of alternative financing have been wiped out.
There is the oil field operator who finds himself being taxed on profits he has not yet made, on business decisions he made under previous budgets, or even on possible future income. He writes: [DOT]
These provisions as contained in the budget are nothing short of legalized extortion.
There is the logging truck operator in southern British Columbia who bought a tandem trailer truck under financing provided through the Small Business Development Bond first introduced in the budget of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). Under the budget of the Minister of Finance, this development bond has been downgraded to a "bail-out" bond, available only to companies in trouble. Since his bank refuses to proceed under the new budget measures, he is left with an expensive piece of equipment, high interest rates and no source of financing.
The Budget-Miss Carney
Then there is the small developer who has been effectively put out of business through the elimination of mortgage reserves. He writes that it normally takes him 10 years to get a subdivision plan approved before he starts to market the property. In the past he usually negotiated a downpayment in cash and then took back a mortgage on the property he sold. He was allowed to declare the profit and pay tax each year as the mortgage payments were made. Now he must declare the entire profit and pay the tax in advance, even though it may be years before he receives his full payment. He wrote to my office as follows:
I was just reaching the stage where lower interest rates made it feasible to start developing some property. Now it wouldn't matter if rates dropped to 5 per cent. I would still be out of business.
Then there is the small developer who has been working for more than a year negotiating the rezoning of his building in a lower mainland municipality. He has written to the minister responsible for housing as follows:
How in the world is an individual supposed to plan in today's economy when you change the rules with no warning and give no time for individuals to prepare or plan their business policy?
There is the Victoria businessman who, with his family, purchased a parcel of land with the intention of developing it as a site for a commercial office building under previous budget provisions. The new budget alters the entire economics of his proposed development. He has been working on his project since November, 1980. He may now be forced to abandon it and face carrying costs of $20,000 per month.
Of course one of the outrageous aspects of the new budget is the provision which taxes accrued income on life insurance policies. In effect, the government proposes to tax income long before it is received. The hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) dealt with this matter earlier this evening.
Then there are all those measures which impact personally on individuals who run their own business or whose union has negotiated employee benefits in the form of dental plans and medical insurance. Under the new budget people receiving such benefits must pay tax on them. One union official advised me that this provision alone could destroy years of work by the union movement in approving the over-all pay package of Canadians. It will also encourage union negotiators to increase wage demands as compensation at a time when the government is asking Canadians to accept lower wages.
Another unfair blow deals with the small businessman who now finds that he cannot utilize his company's deferred profitsharing scheme, his hedge against future years when his earnings may be low. Many small businessmen do not know how much money their companies will earn in a year. Thus they draw very limited salaries and, in the event that there are any profits, they allocate funds to their deferred profit-sharing plan. Now these principals are effectively penalized for setting up their companies, assuming risks and putting their money on the line to create the jobs Canadians need and the goods and services Canadians want. Similarly, the 12.5 per cent tax on dividend contributions to small business will make it harder to finance small business from internal cash flows and increase

December 8, 1981
The Budget-Miss Carney
their reliance on bank financing. Clarkson-Gordon estimated that the dividend tax credit amounts to an increase in income tax of nearly 40 per cent for a small businessman who before the budget took his salary in the form of dividends, if and when he made them. The frustration of many small businessmen is echoed in the one who wrote:
Canada did not attain its present state of prosperity and advancement through a system of penalizing personal initiative.
There is another measure in the budget which hurts individual Canadians, and it deals with income averaging. In the past, individuals who receive severance pay or writers and artists whose annual income varies could roll their funds into income-averaging annuity contracts or registered retirement savings plans. This provision has been eliminated. The result is that the financial security and the retirement plans of many people have been shattered. There are the public servants and other employees who no longer have an opportunity to transfer severance benefits, without tax penalty, into registered retirement savings plans or to use such plans for the purchase of other types of income annuity plans. Initially this tax deferral mechanism was introduced in other budgets to encourage savings and to help people prepare for their retirement years. Now people who planned their entire retirement income under existing budget provisions will also find themselves paying taxes. The fact that they will now be taxed on their retirement allowance means many people will have to rethink their retirement plans. They are also writing to the minister and to their Members of Parliament.
When RRSPs were first introduced in 1957 by Liberal finance minister Walter Harris, he said:
Whatever the subsequent loss of revenue may be, it can, however, be regarded as an indication of the volume of provision being made by Canadians toward freedom from financial worry at a time when their earning power has lessened.
To me, this policy makes good sense. Moreover, the broad effect of this new policy will be anti-inflationary, since it will be an encouragement to increased immediate saving which will be productively employed.
History has shown that Mr. Harris was right; history will show that the Minister of Finance is wrong. The budget provisions which affect income averaging do not just affect the wealthy. They affect farmers who sell their only asset, their farm, and plan to live off the proceeds. Now they too face a heavy tax penalty. They affect thousands of Canadians who bought a registered home ownership savings plan and now realize that they will never be able to buy a house. Before the budget they could roll that money into an income-averaging annuity contract. Now, without any warning, they face the prospect of paying a heavy tax penalty at the time of the rollover. Many people affected by this category have been in touch with me. They are senior citizens who quite simply need the extra money which they must now pay in taxes to keep themselves above the poverty line.
The loss of the general averaging provisions also removes an element of financial stability for people whose incomes vary from year to year. There is a logging operator in northern British Columbia who spent years building up his business. Now, through the elimination of the provision, he will get hit for taxes the first year he meets with any success. There is the
west coast fisherman who did well during this summer's salmon season after several years of poor runs. He operated the whole season under the existing general averaging provisions, and now he feels he will have to pay extra taxes. The loss of this provision hits hard on small business people who earn very little in their first years of operation while they build up their business and then face high taxes in their first good year of operation.
I have attempted to convey some of the views of ordinary Canadians who have been affected by the budget. One of the best views comes from a British Columbian who wrote to the Minister of Finance as follows:
Please explain to me how a budget that creates unemployment, stops construction of housing units, bankrupts the middle class and hamstrings Canadian investors can help Canada at this time.
But I think the best summation of all comes from another British Columbian who wrote the minister as follows:
I'm mad as hell and I'm not gonna take it anymore!
Canadians will not accept the budget. It has caused too much pain, too much anguish and too many broken commitments. The problems are too big for band-aid treatment. The budget must be withdrawn.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in light of what the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney) just said, it would be worth repeating that the minister indicated on a number of occasions that where serious problems are being caused for individuals who made plans and provisions under the old tax rules, he is prepared to consider them seriously and to bring about adjustment provisions for the transition from the old regime to the new regime. It is really unfair to stand in the House of Commons and indicate that the new regime will come into effect immediately without any adjustment or transition provisions, when the minister indicated clearly that such measures would be forthcoming if it could be shown that serious difficulties were being caused for Canadians as a result.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre raised another point and before I get into my discussion I should like to deal with it. The hon. member discussed a great many of the incentives that have been put into the tax system in past years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Loopholes!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Some hon. members opposite say there are loopholes. The same word has been used before. I would say it is an unfortunate word to use, and if I have ever used it myself it was unintentional. Some incentives were put into the tax system in order to achieve certain economic objectives. If those incentives have been used over the years for tax avoidance as opposed to the achievement of economic benefits for Canadians and Canadian taxpayers through the generation of addi-
December 8, 1981

tional wealth, then it behooves the government and this House to ask why they are not achieving their original purpose.
Every time a Canadian taxpayer defers one dollar of tax, that means that other Canadian taxpayers have to take up the burden.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the government spends it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon. members opposite will say that government expenditures should be drastically reduced, and some members on this side and in the corner opposite will agree. We can talk about expenditure restraint, of course, but that does not apply to tax policy. Tax policy is established in order to generate the revenues necessary to finance the operations of government. Given the level of expenditures, the tax policy is then established to raise the revenues sufficient to fund that.
If some people use deferrals or other measures to avoid taxation, it means that other Canadians have to pick up the extra burden. They will pick it up in the form of higher tax rates, as was indicated today by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid); in the form of inflation when the Bank of Canada finances the government deficit, or in the form of higher interest rates when the government has to borrow in the marketplace in order to finance deficits. Certainly, however, the government will have to finance a given level of expenditures. Its operations will be financed and Canadians will have to bear that burden. For every dollar that is rightfully deferred by one Canadian for a good reason, another Canadian has to pick up the additional burden.
Deferrals in the system are a fact of life. If economic benefits greater than the amount of the deferrals themselves are generated, then that is good for Canada. An analysis has to be made, however, and I am sure hon. members opposite would demand it, to determine whether every dollar handed out by the government will return more than one dollar to the Canadian taxpayer.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Show it to us.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a fundamental tenet with which I am sure the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) would agree. I do not argue that it holds true in all cases; I am arguing that it is a fundamental principle, and if the hon. member for York-Peel does not agree, I wish he would say so, but I think he does agree with it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why don't you do it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the federal government or a provincial government decides not to collect certain tax dollars, then some tests have to be made. Over the last two years an analysis has been carried out. In fact it was started by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) who introduced the tax expenditure account in his budget of 1979. That was the first time tax expenditures were examined and listed in a systematic way. They were listed again in 1980. In October of 1980 the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) indicated that he
The Budget-Mr. Evans
intended to examine these expenditures very carefully for his forthcoming budget.
When questions were raised, in some cases it was seen that the incentives were not leading to benefits for the Canadian taxpayer sufficient to justify the non-collection of the revenue which is, by its very nature a tax expenditure. That was the basis on which we started.
I am rather sorry that during these six days of debate we have not had a more careful analysis of the situation that faces this country, the United States, Great Britain and western European countries. The situation that we face, the fundamental problems that we face and the kinds of policies that we will require-

-I wish they would sit back and listen to what I have to say before they criticize it. The circus is at it again, Mr. Speaker.
The fundamental problem in our country-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The fundamental problem is inflation. A number of things flow from an inflationary environment. It increases the uncertainty facing investors and the uncertainty facing consumers. It puts a drag on long-term investment and a drag on economic growth. Time horizons tend to shorten when we are faced with an inflationary environment.

hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), we are not being made aware of the constant interruptions from the gentlemen-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-we saw rising unemployment, we saw high interest rates, we saw no real income growth for Canadians. Essentially, this country, the United States, Britain, France and Germany, all went into a period of stagnation, which is the handmaiden of inflation. Partially due to inflation, during the period from 1967 to 1971, and not only here but also in other countries, there was an increasing burden being placed on the taxpayer caused by the inflationary movement of people rising into higher and higher tax brackets. This further reduced the incentive to work, to save and to invest. By the mid 1970s, all the western countries had recognized the problem and had responded.
However, the typical response of the western countries during the early seventies, mid seventies and late seventies was to try to offset the disincentives being caused by inflation, by an ever-increasing taxation burden, especially in the United States. That is a country which does not currently benefit from indexation of its tax system. These countries tried to respond by increasing the number of tax concessions, by increasing the number of tax credits, by increasing the number of deductions within their systems and, in some countries, such as Canada, by indexation of the tax systems.
However, the real problem was the high marginal tax rates, and those were not touched. The response by the individual countries meant that one could increase the rate of return on investment if one could find an investment vehicle which involved some form of tax concession. That led to greater demand for even more concessions. However, the incentive problem of high marginal tax rates remained, since each additional dollar earned, without an offsetting concession, was taxed at a relatively high rate. Investment for tax policy as opposed to economic reasons became the rule of the day.

However, I think all would agree that, fundamentally, it is the rate of monetary expansion and the growth of purchasing power relative to that which causes inflation.
If we want to solve inflation, we can do it simply through monetary restraint. However, the problem is that when inflation is accelerating, the process of eliminating inflation from one's system through the use of monetary restraint will be long and painful. People will tell us that Japan has high deficits and low inflation. How can that be? It is because Japan's monetary expansion has been relatively low during the period of the last 10 to 15 years; and, in addition to that, it has been able to maintain-

Mr. Speaker, the process could be made faster and less painful if fiscal policy is brought into line with monetary policy on the restraint side. Therefore, as I said, while deficits do not create inflation, they can make the job of the monetary authority more difficult. In other words, the process of moving from a highly inflationary state to a low inflation state without fiscal policy or fiscal restraint will be more painful in terms of higher real interest rates, more painful in high unemployment, and more painful in terms of a longer period of slow growth.
The second fact is that increasing tax burdens, in other words, high marginal tax rates, reduce the incentive to work, save and invest. In other words, they reduce the returns to productive economic activity. Again, I think that this fact is now recognized worldwide, because high marginal tax rates, if one takes the British example, have led to tax avoidance behaviour, have led to the growth of the underground economy and have led to the kinds of demands for more tax concessions. The same kinds of demands were being seen and felt here in Canada. First of all-

They tend to direct investment and savings into areas where they might not have gone otherwise. It narrows and erodes the tax base which, as I said earlier, necessitates the placing of a heavier tax burden on other Canadian taxpayers, and it reallocates the tax burden generally on to those who are less vocal and less well organized. It is very important, I think that where the term loophole has arisen in the past, it has led to a perception by individuals in our society of inequity and a demand for ever more concessions by individuals and groups.

speechtext:
-was brought into place. These are the fundamental facts which are at the heart of our economic difficulties in this country, namely, inflation, and the rates of taxation and deficits.
What of the current policy implemented by the budget? The budget we have in place is one of monetary restraint. There has been a policy of gradualism to bring down the rate of growth and money supply over a good many years now. It is now at the level where we can expect to see some break in the rate of inflation. However, as the Governor of the Bank of Canada has said, some support on the fiscal side is required if we are not to go through a prolonged period of difficulty. Therefore, the government has introduced a policy of fiscal restraint. At the same time, it has tried to improve the over-all incentives, not the specific incentives, in our system of working, saving and investing.
Now, for obvious reasons in politics, the opposition will say that there is no fiscal restraint.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A twelve billion dollar deficit!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
An honest and objective appraisal of the situation will show that to be false. I think it is fair to ask Canadians to consider the public accounts figures. During a period of transition from a highly inflationary period to a low inflationary period, when we can expect real interest rates to be higher than we expect them to be over the medium term, we can look at government discretionary expenditures, if you will, not expenditures as given in the public accounts without public debt charges. The figures in the public accounts for growth of net government expenditures without public debt charges show, and show clearly, that there has been and there continues to be a policy of restraint of discretionary government expenditures. The question is whether the transition costs- and that is the argument we will get into with regard to national account versus public accounts-those costs that are associated with the move from a highly inflationary situation,
a high unemployment situation, a slow growth situation toward lower inflation, lower unemployment and a faster growth situation, should be considered as part of the government's permanent expenditure pattern. That is where the argument arises. I say it is not fair and it is not honest to the Canadian people to include those transition costs on a permanent basis in the government's expenditures as part of the government expenditures.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Someone has to.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Certainly they are not permanent costs. They are not discretionary costs. That is especially the case with regard to interest rates. When interest rates rose dramatically over the last year, the cost of servicing the public debt went up by some $2.5 billion. This was totally unanticipated. This was a transitional cost that one cannot say was an intentional result of government policy.
I would doubt whether the Opposition would give the government credit when interest rates come down, if the public debt charges come down and government expenditures fall as a result of those lower debt charges. People would say, "See, the government is now constraining its expenditures." Instead, the opposition will say "No, this happened because interest rates fell, not because of discretion". But I say it is fair on both sides.
I contend that we have put forward a policy of balanced restraint conducive to the fight against inflation. Given what is happening around the world and the domestic situation that we face now, the agreed need is for restraint. I do not think there is any argument on either side of the House that there is a need for restraint, that there is a need to support monetary policy, that there is a need to fight inflation. The question is, how do we achieve it? We can do this in one or two ways. We can cut expenditures. But where would we cut expenditures?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

The hon. member for York-Peel is an example of one who would cut government expenditures. That indicates to me that if that is the best he could do, which is a sizeable sum-and I am not saying it is not-we are talking about $5 billion over 5 years, Mr. Speaker, and we are talking about a federal deficit today of about $10 billion. We are not talking about a major decrease from that kind of expenditure reduction.
From where would the expenditure reductions come? Would hon. members slash the social security of Canadians? Are those the programs they would slash?

-she has decided that she would cut social expenditures and let the monetary policy carry the load over the long period. You have seen the unemployment effect of that. Our government has decided that the approach to take to improving incentive and reducing the deficit is to broaden the tax base, to shore up the foundations of the tax base, to ensure that the tax burden is carried by a greater number of Canadians in an equitable fashion. That will generate the revenues. That will allow us to preserve the valuable system of social programs that we have built up in this country over the years. That will allow us to cut the tax rate which will increase the incentives to work, save and invest.
That approach which is being implemented by this government, I contend, will prove to be successful. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it will prove to be successful and it will be copied by other governments in the western world as a way of coming to grips with these problems without placing the burden on those least able to carry that burden.
The budget attacks the root causes of our problems. It supports the monetary policy in the fight against inflation. It puts strong general incentives in place to work, save and invest by cutting marginal tax rates. An additional benefit, and a benefit that is not recognized as flowing from this budget, but should be, is that because of the reduced deficit and because of the higher and higher incentives, we will have lower rates of

understanding of what was provided for in the budget. As a matter of fact, I defy members of the Department of Finance to say what are the implications of this budget as far as the Canadian public is concerned.
The Minister of Finance was proud to announce that this budget had three themes: restraint, equity and economic renewal. In relation to restraint, I call attention to the table at page 60 of "The Budget in More Detail". As my colleague, the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), and others have said, expenditures have increased by 22 per cent. That is restraint? Revenues by the Government of Canada increased by 19.6 per cent this year. We know that this increases tremendously through income taxes, and if the Canadian people think the minister is being easy in respect of personal income taxes, let me point out that this year he projects revenue through personal income tax to be $23,665 billion. In three years' time that is projected at $41,470 billion. That is restraint? Corporate income tax revenue almost doubles. Petroleum and gas revenue taxes go up almost five times. We find this all the way down the line. As a matter of fact, total budgetary revenues under this budget of restraint will go up from $54,310 billion to $64,960 billion next year. From that minor and modest sum, total budgetary revenues for 1985-86 are projected to be $91,745 billion. That is the projection in respect of budgetary revenues on the basis of tax rates and the national energy plan. The government has fashioned three more udders to the cow this year and has taken the teats from two udders to itself. Is that what is said to be restraint by government?
People like the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and other ministers have nothing else in mind but spending programs, which they put forward before their docile colleagues and which they convince a part of the Canadian public to buy. Then they say they must have the money. They do not think first about getting the money and then bringing in the programs. No, they get the programs into place and then insist that they have the money. This is why we have this pulling and pushing with the provinces. The Government of Canada says it must have money and it says how it is going to get the money. That is restraint?
As far as equity is concerned, every discredited proposition contained in the Carter report and every discredited proposition in the white paper on taxation in 1969 has been brought forward by the tax policy section of the Department of Finance, where all the senior people have gone, and we are left with this miserable, mean group of proposals we find in this budget. We will see whether there is equity and we will see what this does to Canadians. Even our professional athletes are going to flee from us.
